It is said that Lord Hanuman had performed tapas at this kshethram. When the Lord appeared in front of him, Lord Hanuman asked the Lord to re-enact the scene of Gajendra Moksham. 

The story of Gajendra Moksham is as follows. King Indradyumna was a renowned ruler of the Pandya Dynasty. It is said that he was the one who constructed the Puri Jagannath Temple. One day, the King was engaged in deep meditation when Sage Agastya visited the Kingdom and sought hospitality from the king. The King was so deep in his meditation that he overlooked the Sage. The sage got irritated and cursed the king, saying he would be reborn as an elephant. Similarly, a Gandharva named Huhu was cursed by Sage Devala to turn into a crocodile as he attempted to break the Sage’s penance. Many years passed, and King Indradyumna reincarnated as an elephant who had once been the ruler of an elephant herd on the Mountain of Trikuta. Gajendra used to visit a lake on the mountain daily and offer the Lord a lotus as dakshina every day. On one such visit to the lake, a crocodile caught Gajendra’s leg. This crocodile was none other than the cursed Huhu. Gajendra started to wail in pain and called out to the Lord by holding up a lotus that he had just plucked to give to the Lord. Gajendra referred to the Lord as “Aadhimoola” and called out a plea for help. All the gods saw Gajendra's plight, but when they heard the call, Aadhimoola refused to help him as they were not qualified to do justice to that title. It is said that as soon as Lord Sriman Narayana heard the call of the devotee, he didn’t even wait for Garuda. He ran at the top of his speed, and soon Garuda caught up and took the Lord to the Trikuta mountain, where the Lord’s Sudarshana Chakra had already taken off, even before he could release it. The chakra killed the crocodile and released Huhu from the curse. It is also said that the lotus held by the Lord is the same Lotus that Gajendra presented to the Lord that day. Following this, Gajendra was granted moksham.

Legend has it that Devi Lakshmi was born as Vanchulavalli at the foot of a Vanchula tree to Medhavi Muni. Lord Vishnu is believed to have manifested himself in the Pancha Vyuha forms and married Vanchulavalli Thayaar. In the sanctum, one finds the idols of the deities – Sankarshanan in the east, Pradyumnan in the south, Anirudhan in the west, Purushottaman in the north, and Vasudevan in the center.
It is said that the Lord had performed Pancha-Samskaram for Tirumangai Azhwar at this kshethram. The story is as follows:
Tirumangai Azhwar wanted to marry a woman named Kumudhavalli. She placed two conditions, namely, 1) to get Pancha-Samskaram done, and 2) to perform tadhiyararadhanam (annadhanam) for a thousand people for one year. Tirumangai Azhwar satisfied the second condition, but when it came to fulfilling the first condition, no acharya was ready to perform Pancha-Samskaram, as Tirumangai Azhwar was a very fierce personality. Thus Tirumangai Azhwar approached the Lord here, and the Lord himself performed the Pancha-Samskaram. Hence, we can see the Lord holding his arms out with the Panchajanyam in His right hand and the Sudharshanam in His left hand.


***This temple is regarded as a Mani Mada Mantapam, which means the temple is divided into partitions known as mantapams, wherein one must climb up a flight of stairs to move from one mantapam to the next to reach the garbha griha, which is placed internally. As one moves closer to the main garbha griha, we can see a shrine outside the garbha griha dedicated to Kal Garudan. There is a peculiarity with Garudan here. At any other kshethram, one can find a Garuda Vahanam made of wood or panchaloha, but at this kshethram, we see a Garuda made of saligrama shila. Another peculiarity is when Garudar comes out for uthsavam. As Kal Garudan comes out of the shrine, we see that four people hold up Garudar. As the first mantapam is crossed, eight people are required to carry Garudar. Similarly, by the time Garudar reaches the temple gates, sixty-four people carry Garudar. As Garudar makes his journey back to the shrine again, only four are needed to place Garudar back in the shrine. 

Anyone afflicted by sarpa-dosham is said to be relieved of those impediments by the Garudan here at this kshetram.

Hiranyaksha’s brother Hiranyakashipu was a great demon emperor who dominated the

earth. He performed great penance to Lord Brahma. After centuries of penance, Brahma

finally appeared in front of Hiranyakashipu and asked told him that he had appeared to

grant him a boon for the penance that Hiranyakashipu had performed. Hiranyakashipu

asked for immortality. Brahma said it was against the law of nature and that it was not in

his power to grant this boon and asked him to rethink what he desired. Hiranyakashipu

thought for a while and asked for a boon that would be equivalent to immortality. He asked

that he shouldn’t be killed by man nor animal, not be killed inside the house nor outside,

not be killed at day nor at night, not be killed in space nor on the surface of the earth.

Further, he should not be killed by anything which was created by Brahma. Brahma

granted this and disappeared. Soon Hiranyakashipu became a tyrant and became a ruthless

king. He soon had a son by the name of Prahalada. Prahalada was a great devotee of Lord

Vishnu. Hiranyakashipu considered Lord Vishnu as his mortal enemy as he had incarnated

himself to kill his brother Hiranyaksha. When Prahalada was in his mother’s womb, Sage

Narada had narrated tales of the Lord to his mother. As the mother heard the stories, so did

the fetus. When Prahalada was admitted to Gurukulam, he changed the views of all his


teachers and all the students to advise them to praise the Lord instead of praising his

father. When Hiranyakashipu came to know of the events that were taking place in the

Gurukulam, he took measures to try and kill his son. He tried to get him trampled by an

elephant, feed him poison, imprison him without food, throw him into a ravaging flame.

None of his methods produced the results that he wanted. He then brings Prahalada to his

royal court. He asked him how he was surviving all the deadly situations. He said the Lord

was protecting him. He also said that the Lord is within everyone, including his father.

Hiranyakashipu then drew his mace and pointed out to a pillar and asked him if his Lord

was present in that particular pillar. When Prahalada said yes, Hiranyakashipu smashed

the pillar, and from that pillar, the Lord emerged in the form of a man-lion. The incarnation

had the face of a lion and the body of a man. The Lord’s rage knew no bounds. He dragged

Hiranyakashipu to the doorstep and sat on the separating junction, which is neither inside

nor outside the home. The Lord placed Hiranyakashipu on his lap, which was neither in

space nor on Earth. Then the Lord used his nails at a time of sunset, which was neither day

nor night, and dug into the stomach of Hiranyakashipu, ripping out his intestines and

putting an end to the tyrant.


The legend has it that Garuda was desirous of seeing Lord Vishnu in His Narasimha

avataram; thus, he meditated upon Him at the Ugra Sthambham, and the Lord manifested

Himself as nine forms of Narasimha.


1. BHARGAVA NARASIMHA SWAMY

The Bhargava Narasimha Swamy is situated at a distance of two kilometers from the Lower

Ahobilam, on a hill, near the sacred pond, known as ‘Bhargava Theertham,’ where Bhargava



Rama(Parashurama) performed his penance. Hence the Lord of the temple is known as

Bhargava Narasimha Swamy.




2. YOGANANDA NARASIMHA SWAMY

This temple is to the southeast of Lower Ahobilam at a distance of 2 kilometers. The

popular legend is that after killing Hiranyakasipu, Lord Narasimha taught Prahlada several

yogic postures. Therefore, the Lord in this aspect is called Yogananda Narasimha.





3. CHATRAVATA NARASIMHA SWAMY

About three kilometers from lower Ahobilam, the image of the deity is installed under a

peepal tree, surrounded by thorny bushes. Hence, the Lord is called Chatravata Narasimha

Swamy. The Lord can be seen putting thaalam with one of His hands. It is said that the Lord

is enjoying the musical service of two yakshas named Haha and Huhu.





4. AHOBILA NARASIMHA SWAMY

The temple, situated on the Upper Ahobilam, at a distance of eight kilometers from the

Lower Ahobilam, is the main temple and the earliest of all the nine temples there. The Lord

here appears in his fierce aspect, called Ugra Narasimha, who is the presiding deity of the

temple and is known as Ahobila Nrisimha Swamy. It is firmly believed that Lord Narasimha

was ‘Swayambhu’ (self-manifest) here.




5. KRODAKARA (VARAHA) NARASIMHA SWAMY

The temple of this Lord is one kilometer away from the main temple of Ahobila Nrisimha

Swamy on the Upper Ahobilam. The image of the deity has the face of a boar (Varaha or

kroda), and the Lord is seen along with his Consort, Lakshmi. Hence the Lord of the temple

is known as Krodakara (Varaha) Narasimha Swamy here.





6. KARANJA NARASIMHA SWAMY

This shrine is situated at a distance of one kilometer from the Upper Ahobilam and one

furlong from the road leading to Lower Ahobilam. The image of the deity is installed under

a tree called ‘Karanja Vruksham.’ Hence this Lord is called Karanja Narasimha Swamy. The

Lord here is prathyaksham to Hanuman. It is said that when Hanuman performed tapas

here at this kshethram, Lord Narasimha appeared with a bow and arrow, signifying that He

is Rama.





7. MALOLA NARASIMHA SWAMY

Nearly two kilometers from the main temple of Upper Ahobilam is the famous shrine of

Malola Narasimha Swamy. The deity here appears in ‘Soumya’ (graceful) form. As Lord

Narasimha is seen with his consort, Lakshmi, He is known as Malola Narasimha Swamy.

The word ‘Malola’ means beloved to Lakshmi (Ma=Lakshmi, Lola= beloved). It is said that

the ‘utsavamoorthi’ of the Lord appeared to Srimath Adivan Satakopa Jeeyar, the first

Jeeyar of Ahobila Mutt. Right from the founder, i.e., the first Jeeyar of Ahobila Mutt down to

the 44th pontiff, Srivan Satakopa Sri Vedanta Desika Yatheendra Mahadesika, the present

jeeyar, the utsavamoorthi of Malola Narasimha Swamy is worshipped, and it is taken by

them whenever they are on religious tours, visiting the villages every year. Recently, the

45th Jeeyar Srivan Satakopa Sri Narayana Yatheendra Mahadesikan has taken over the

worship.





8. JWALA NARASIMHA SWAMY

The temple of Jwala Nrisimha Swamy lies higher up the above temple, on a hill called

‘Achalachaya Meru.’ This is about four kilometers from the Upper Ahobilam temple. This

place is said to be the actual spot where the fierce anger of the Lord reached its culmination

when he tore Hiranyakasipu.





9. PAVANA NARASIMHA SWAMY

Nearby the above time is the shrine of Pavana Narasimha, on the banks of the river, Pavana,

and it is about six kilometers from the Upper Ahobilam temple. Hence the Lord of the

shrine is known as Pavana Narasimha Swamy. It is said that Mahalakshmi reincarnated

Herself as Chenchulakshmi into one of the local tribes that resided here. When Lord

Narasimha was roaming the land in enraged after killing Hiranyakashipu, Chenchulakshmi

is said to have pacified the Lord and married Him.





UGRA STHAMBHAM

At a distance of eight kilometers from the Upper Ahobilam temple, we can see a cleft of the

mountain dividing it into two visible parts. It is a long-held view that from the cleft, the

Lord appeared in the form of Narasimha, and this cleft is known as ‘Ugra Sthambham.’

The idol as we see it today is said to have originated from the milky oceans of Sri Vaikuntham. Lord Brahma then took the idol to worship, and for many eons, was worshipped by Lord Brahma in Satyalokam. A time came when the great king Ikshvaku approached Lord Brahma and asked him to install the idol of the Lord in Bhoolokam. Considering the king’s request, Lord Brahma obliged and installed the idol of the Lord along with the Pranavaakara Vimanam at Ayodhya, along the banks of the river Saryu. The Lord then remained in Ayodhya even till Lord Rama was the king of Ayodhya. After the battle with Ravana, the Lord returned to Ayodhya to be coronated formally. Here, he gifted all his army generals with something unique and meaningful. When Vibishana’s turn came during the distribution of divine gifts after Lord Rama’s victory over Ravana, he humbly requested Lord Rama to give him the idol of Sri Ranganathar so that he could take it back to Lanka for worship. Lord Rama, recognizing Vibishana's unwavering devotion and righteousness, agreed without hesitation. Thus, the divine idol, along with the Pranavakara Vimanam—a sanctified structure shaped in the form of the sacred syllable Pranavam (a-u-m)—was entrusted to Vibishana, who then began his journey southward aboard the Pushpaka Vimanam. As Vibishana reached the sacred banks of the river Cauvery, it was the auspicious month of Panguni. According to the ancient traditions upheld by Lord Rama and his Ikshvaku lineage, this period marked the celebration of the grand Brahmotsavam festival. In reverence to this dharmic custom, Vibishana paused his journey and conducted a nine-day festival in honor of the Lord on the riverbank. During the course of these festivities, the idol and the Pranavakara Vimanam were placed at a site later known as Sesha Peetam, near the sacred tank Chandrapushkarani. But when Vibishana attempted to resume his journey, he found the Vimanam immovable—it had firmly anchored itself to the earth. Overcome with grief and confusion, Vibishana was then graced with a divine vision of Lord Vishnu, who appeared before him. The Lord consoled His devotee, declaring that He had chosen this very spot to be His eternal abode. He assured Vibishana that although He would remain in Bharata Varsha, He would face southward toward Lanka as a mark of blessing and everlasting connection. Touched by this revelation, Vibishana accepted the divine will with devotion and humility. It is believed that to this day, Vibishana comes at midnight to offer his prayers to Lord Ranganathar in an invisible, celestial form. Thus, the reclining Lord of Srirangam, ensconced in the Pranavakara Vimanam that embodies the essence of the Pranavam (a-u-m), took His place on the banks of the Cauvery by His own will. This sacred event established Srirangam as the foremost among the 108 Divya Desams—a sanctum where divine grace, eternal dharma, and boundless devotion converge. This temple is enormous in size and is the largest temple complex, spanning 156 acres, surrounded by seven concentric walls (the outermost wall has a perimeter of over 3 km) and 21 gopurams. agreed without hesitation. Thus, the divine idol, along with the Pranavakara Vimanam—a

sanctified structure shaped in the form of the sacred syllable Pranavam (a-u-m)—was

entrusted to Vibishana, who then began his journey southward aboard the Pushpaka

Vimanam.

This kshethram is the avatara sthalam for both Periya Azhwar and Sri Andal.
In the then Pandya kingdom, there was a small town called Putthoor, where great scholars and pundits were residing. Nearby, there was a forest where hunters were living. The chief of these hunters had two sons named Villi and Kandan. One day, Villi and Kandan went to the forest for hunting as usual. They spotted a tiger, and it escaped the arrows from their bows. Kandan started chasing vigorously and went deep into the forest. After some time, the tiger hid behind a tree and pounced on Kandan, killing him. Villi waited for his brother for a long time and started searching for him. When he spotted the dead body of his brother, his heart almost stopped with grief, and he cried heavily and fell unconscious on his brother’s body. During his unconsciousness, he had a scene in front of his eyes; Sriman Narayana, along with Mahalakshmi, appeared and instructed Villi to stop lamenting. They told him that They would bring his brother back to life. The two brothers would then search for a giant banyan tree in the middle of the forest, where they would find Lord Vatapatrashayee, who had been lying there for a very long time. The divine couple also told Villi that they would find a cave nearby with treasures that one could never even dream of. They further instructed that the brothers were to use that wealth to deforest the area and construct a magnificent temple that had never been seen before. Saying this, the Divine couple disappeared. When Villi came back to consciousness, he did not know whether what he saw (in his unconscious state) was true at all, and was confused. But suddenly, Kandan got up alive as if he had just woken up from sleep (without any wounds even). Villi explained the whole thing to his brother, and both of them hugged each other for having been blessed by the Lord and having been chosen by the Lord to establish the temple.

Soon, many Vaishnava scholars began to migrate towards Putthoor, among them  Mukunda Bhattar and his wife, Padmavalli. The couple was ardent devotees of Sri Vatapatrashayee. On an auspicious day, the couple was blessed with a son, named Vishnuchittar. The child lived up to his name by constantly finding ways to contemplate how to find the Lord’s days. As time passed, he would perform pushpa-kainkaryam to Sri Vatapatrashayee. As he aged, he sold his property. He purchased a small plot of land near the temple, which he converted into a Nandavanam, where he cultivated various creepers, vines, fragrant flowers, and tulasi plants. The plot also featured a small pond with crystal-clear water. Vishnuchittar would spend his time cultivating his garden, plucking the flowers, and making garlands for the Lord. Over time, his small plot was allowed to expand and transform into a vast, flourishing garden with a lovely scent due to all the flowers that bloomed within it. Soon, he married a woman who shared his ideals of serving the Lord. 

During that time, there was a king named Vallabhadevan, whose capital was situated in Madurai. He was an ardent devotee of Lord Vishnu and wished to learn the meaning of the Vedas and Upanishads. He enquired with his chief minister as to how he could achieve this goal. The minister suggested that the king call all the Vedic Scholars present in his kingdom to debate and question all the matters present in the Vedas and Upanishads. The one who could solve all the questions posed by the king would be rewarded dearly. The king agreed with the minister’s suggestion, and soon an announcement was made throughout the kingdom saying there would be a grand meeting of all the Vedic Scholars in the land. The scholar who would impress the king with their answers would be rewarded with gold coins, which would be hung in a divine binding. The coins would present themselves to the person who would aptly answer all of the king’s questions. Many scholars came before the king, but none gave satisfactory answers that the king desired. One night, Lord Vatapatrashayee appeared in Vishnuchittar‘s dreams and instructed him to go to the king’s court to claim the prize that was being offered. Vishnuchittar told the Lord that he knew nothing about the Vedas or Upanishads. All he knew to do was to make garlands and present them to the Lord. The Lord then told Vishnuchittar not to worry and to go to the royal court. The Lord said He would speak through the mouth of Vishnuchittar. That same night, the Lord also appeared in the dreams of the chief minister and asked him to make royal arrangements to receive Vishnuchittar and escort him to the king’s court. 

The next morning, a royal elephant with palanquins arrived and carried Vishnuchittar to the royal court. As he entered, all the scholars began to murmur and pass sarcastic comments about him, knowing that his knowledge was limited. Vishnuchittar prostrated himself before the king and the gathered scholars, and then began his speech on the Vedas and Upanishads. As and when the king questioned, it was almost as though the answer to the question was pre-prepared and ready. Finally, to close his speech, Vishnuchittar made a final statement that said, “Sriman Narayanane Paramporul.” This translates to “It is Lord Sriman Narayana who is the only protector, and it is with His blessing that the universe is surviving. It is He and only He who is the underlying principle that is mentioned in the four Vedas and Upanishads. When this statement was made, the binding came undone, and the gold coins showered into Vishnuchittar‘s hands from above. The king was overcome with joy and ecstasy. All the gathered scholars lowered their heads in shame. The king then asked Vishnuchittar how he had spoken about all the Vedas and Upanishads in such simple language. Vishnuchittar then told the king that truly it was he who had spoken and that the Lord himself intended for this to perspire. The king was deeply moved by what Vishnuchittar said and fell to his feet. He arranged for complete royal honors and sent him around the kingdom in a royal procession. At one point, when Vishnuchittar looked up at the sky, he saw the Lord along with Mahalakshmi seated atop Garudan, granting their blessing to him. It was at that moment that, with eyes filled with tears of joy, he said the words“pallaandu, pallaandu pallayiratthandu palakodi noorayiram.” These words are still sung to date during sathumorai seva every day, whether it may be at a temple or within a household. 

Periya Azhwar being taken on the royal procession and seeing the Lord and Mahalakshmi

Life went back to normal for Vishnuchittar, and he continued his pushpa-kainkaryam for Lord Vatapatrashayee. Once, while plucking flowers in the garden, he found a child on a flower in the garden and named her Andal and brought her up in the service of the Lord. One day, Periya Azhwar(Vishnuchittar) found Andal wearing the garland meant for the Lord. Discarding that garland, he prepared fresh garlands and offered them to the Lord. PeriaAzhwar was surprised to see the Lord refusing to accept the garland except the one used by Andal. Hence, Andal is called Shoodi Kudutha Nachiyar. As per the wishes of the Lord, Periya Azhwar gave Andal in marriage to Sri Ranganathar in Sri Rangam, and Andal, on entering the sanctum, merged with the Lord.

Sri Andal Nachiyar

Sri Andal is said to be the reincarnation of Bhoodevi. When Lord Varaha saved Bhoodevi from the grasp of Hiranyaksha, He is said to have delivered various Brahma-gyanam to Bhoodevi. It is noted that Bhoodevi came in this form to provide that knowledge to the people in a way that they would understand it simply. Thus, Sri Andal wrote 30 Pasurams known as Tirupavai and Nachiyar Tirumozhi, which contain 143 Pasurams that convey all the knowledge that was given by Sri Varaha Perumal to Bhoodevi on that day.
Even to date, on the tirunakshtram of Sri Andal, Tiruaadipooram Utsavam is observed on a very grand scale. This is the time when brahmotsavam is done here, and a massive number of devotees throng to see this grand celebration.

Tiruaadipooram Celebration

Legend tells the story of Salihotra Maharishi, who had his hermitage in this place. He used to grind rice for a living and offered half of the flour to the seekers, while he consumed the rest himself. He was an ardent devotee of Lord Vishnu. To test his devotion, the Lord appeared as a guest to him one day. He requested Salihotra Maharishi to offer him food, which the sage did. The guest felt hungry and requested the sage to provide more food. The sage offered the other half of the flour, which he used to consume himself. The guest asked for a place to rest(Evvul), and the sage readily offered his hermitage. On arriving at the hermitage, the guest revealed His true form and blessed the sage. 

*** This kshethram has a few specialties. It is said that if one bathes in the Hruthapanashini Pushkarani on Thai Ammavasi, all of their ailments will be cured. Another belief that has seen fruit here is when a person takes a handful of jaggery and dissolves it in the water on any Ammavasi, all their wishes come true. 
When Lord Shiva had Brahmahatya dosham for killing Daksha Prajapati, it is said that after he bathed in this Pushkarani, all his sins were absolved. 
Another story tells the story of the Lord’s marriage to Vasumathi Thayaar. It is said that Thayaar belonged to a village called Dharmasenapuram, located near Tiruvallur. Vasumathi Thayaar was the daughter of the king of Dharmasenapuram. She wanted to get married to the Lord. Her father agreed, but he had a condition: his Son-in-law should not leave his kingdom and take his daughter with him. The Lord agreed to this condition and promised the king that He would never leave Tiruvallur.

This Naimisaranyam is said to be the place where most of the rishis performed sacrifices, tapas, and meditation, and explained the meaning of the old Puranas and Vedas. One day, Kadru and Vinata were arguing about the color of Ucchaishravas' tail. Vinata claimed that the divine horse was a pure white color throughout, but Kadru said the horse’s body was white, but the tail was black. Thus, the two had a bet to see who was right. The one who would lose the bet would become the other’s slave. Kadru knew very well that the tail of Ucchaishravas was pure white, and knowing she would lose the bet, she told her sons to wrap themselves around the tail of Ucchaishravas so that she could win the bet. One day, in the presence of Kadru and Vinata, Ucchaishravas passed by with a black tail. Thus, Kadru won the bet, enslaving Vinata. For five hundred years, Vinata was a slave to Kadru. After five hundred years, Vinata’s second egg hatched, and from that egg was born Garudan. As soon as he was born, he went straight to his aunt and demanded that his mother be freed from slavery.
To this, Kadru put a condition, saying that if Garudan could bring the Amruthakalasham (the divine pitcher that contained the sacred nectar of immortality) for her and her children, she would release Vinata from slavery. Thus, Garudan immediately left for Swargalokam and defeated all the Devas in battle, successfully retrieving the Amruthakalasham. After retrieving the Amruthakalasham, Garudan returned to Bhulokam. On Bhulokam, Lord Vishnu was very impressed with Garudan for his strength and dedication. The Lord then offered Garudan a boon. Garudan asked that he should always be soaring far above the Lord; thus, Garudan is present in the Dwajasthambham outside the temple. The Lord also then told Garudan that he wanted Garudan to be constantly under his command; therefore, he asked Garudan to become his vaahanam. The Lord also relieved Vinata from slavery and took the Amruthakalasham. The Lord is said to have taken the Amruthakalasham, placed it on His head, and danced. Hence, he got the name Kudamaadukoothan.
Another story tells us that, after the Mahabharata battle, as the Lord was on his way back to Dwarka from his tour of South India, the Lord reached Arimeya Vinnagaram, where Utanka Maharishi’s ashram was situated at the time. Utanka Maharishi, upon seeing the Lord, is said to have stopped the Lord’s chariot and asked him to visit his Ashramam. When the Lord reached the Ashramam, Utanka Maharishi began to pose indirect questions to the Lord about how He ensured the Pandavas won the battle. The Lord sensed that the Maharishi had other intentions and asked him what he had in mind. Utanka Maharishi then told the Lord that he desired to see the Vishwaroopa Darshanam as He had shown Arjuna. The Lord then showed the Maharishi His Vishwaroopam.

Before Lord Athi Vardar was presented the havis to the yagnam, Saraswati Devi presented many interruptions to stop the yagnam from reaching completion. Saraswati Devi is said to have summoned many different types of demons, ghosts, and ghouls to attack the yagna-kundam. Lord Brahma is said to have appealed to Lord Vishnu to appear and protect the yagnam so that it would achieve its completion. The Lord is said to have appeared with eight hands (Ashtabhujar), holding weapons in seven hands and a lotus in one hand, symbolizing that he would attack his enemies while also protecting his devotees. The Lord is said to have vanquished all the interruptions placed by Devi Saraswati in her first attempt to foil the performance of the yagnam.
The Lord here is referred to as Gajendravaradhan, as He is said to have shown Pey Azhwar the sight of Gajendra Moksham here at this kshethram.

*** A peculiarity of this kshethram is that this is the only temple in all the Divyadesams at Kanchipuram to house a Vaikuntha Dwaram. Usually, if the entrance of the temple is east-facing, the Vaikuntha Dwaram is placed in a west-facing direction. But here, the Vaikuntha Dwaram and the temple entrance are both facing in the easterly direction.

During the Mahabharata war, on the fifteenth day of the war, Bheema and Drishtadyumna attacked Dronacharya in full fury, but it had no avail. Drona still had many divine weapons left in his Astra-Bhandara. Then Krishna devised a plan wherein Drona would voluntarily drop his weapons, thereby presenting the opportunity for the Pandavas to kill him. Krishna told Bheema to kill an elephant named Ashvatthama, and then told everyone on the battlefield to announce that Ashvatthama was dead. As instructed, Bheema immediately killed Ashvatthama, the elephant, and all the warriors in the Pandavas' army started screaming, saying Ashvatthama was dead. When Drona heard these words, he was in disbelief. He immediately went to Yudhisthira and asked what all the warriors were saying was true. Yudhisthira was put in a spot at that moment. He went into deep thought about how to convey the information. He says अश्वत्थामा हत: which translates to Ashvatthama is dead. As soon as he had lied, the chariot, which always used to hover four inches above the ground, immediately fell to the ground. Drona was heartbroken and laid down his arms, renouncing war. He assumed a yogic stance and prayed to Lord Vishnu, then instructed Karna to take charge of the army and protect Duryodhana.
As soon as Drona had laid down his arms, Drishtadyumna came and beheaded Drona. 
It is said that Yudhisthira came to this kshethram, bathed in the Chitraaru river, and performed tapas to the Lord here. The Lord appeared in front of Yudhisthira and gave him atonement for his sin of lying to Dronacharya. 

*** An interesting point that can be seen here is that the Lord holds the Panchajanyam in the right hand and the Sudharshanam in the left hand.

on the battlefield to announce that Ashvatthama was dead. As instructed, Bheema

immediately killed Ashvatthama, the elephant, and all the warriors on the Pandavas army

started screaming, saying Ashvatthama was dead. When these words were heard by Drona,

he was in disbelief. He immediately went to Yudhisthira and asked if what all the warriors

were saying was true or not. Yudhisthira was put in a spot at that moment. He went into


deep thought as to how to relay the information. He says अ.व"थामा हत: which translates to


Ashvatthama is dead. As soon as he had lied, the chariot, which always used to hover four

inches above the ground, immediately fell to the ground. Drona was heartbroken and laid

down his arms, and renounced war. He took to a yogic stance and prayed to Lord Vishnu,

Ganga and Kaveri started to argue. Ganga claimed that she was a greater entity than Kaveri. To solve this feud, both of the devis went to Lord Brahma. The Lord appeared and showed her Vishwaroopa Darshanam, but this did not satisfy her. The Lord then showed her His form as He appears in Sri Vaikuntham and told her that soon He would lie in Bujanga Shayanam at Sri Rangam, and she would flow by His Tiruvadi (His holy lotus feet) until the end of Kali Yuga, thereby making her a greater entity than Ganga.

*** Here, the Lord can be seen with five of his spouses, namely, Sri Devi, Bhoodevi, Neela Devi, Mahalakshmi, and Saranayaki Thayaar.

There are multiple legends associated with this temple. Let’s go through them one by one.
How the Lord appeared:
Lord Mahavishnu is said to have defeated the demon brothers, Madhu and Kaitabha. When He defeated them, their blood is said to have spilled over the earth, causing the world to smell with a very foul odor. Bhoomi Devi is said to have performed tapas at this kshethram to relieve Herself of the odor. The Lord is said to have answered Her tapas and appeared here for the first time. Vishwakarma is said to have designed the temple here. Over time and improper maintenance, the Lord is said to have gotten buried under the earth. Many years passed, and the Lord was forgotten. Then came a king named Karya Maharaja, who had no children. The king was growing anxious as he grew older, and he did not have any children.
One night, the Lord appeared in the king’s dream and told him that He wanted to be reestablished in the temple. The Lord directed the king to Nanguneri and told him where He lay buried below the earth. The king began digging and, at one point, saw that the tip of one of his tools had blood on it. Upon closer inspection, the king found the Lord, Sri Devi, Bhoomi Devi, Suryan, Chandran, Brighu Maharishi, Markandeya Maharishi, Urvashi, Thilothama, Vishwaksenar, and Garudan. (Among all the Swayam Vyaktha Kshethrams, this is the only kshethram where there have been 11 vigrahams that have emerged.) The king was bamboozled by the blood and did not mean to hurt the Lord in any way. The king immediately begged for the Lord’s forgiveness. The Lord told the king not to be worried and asked him to apply some gingelly oil, and the wound would heal. The king followed the Lord’s instructions. To date, this tradition is still observed, where the Lord is massaged with a mixture of gingelly oil and sandalwood oil, along with a blend of medicinal herbs, and abhishekam is performed daily.

Yennai Kannar

After the abhishekam is performed, all the oil is collected and poured into a well that is 25 feet deep. This well is known as the yennai kannar. The oil from this well ages over time and undergoes multiple chemical reactions when exposed to sunlight. All devotees who visit this kshethram take some amount of this oil with them to their households without fail. This oil has multiple medicinal benefits, including the ability to alleviate arthritis symptoms, and it can also be used to treat leprosy.
Another legend goes that once upon a time, there was a righteous king in the kingdom of Sind named Gunaseelan. In his usual pastime, he went out hunting, followed by his attendants on horseback. The King missed his companions in the trackless forest, and when he was feeling the pinch of thirst and hunger, he could locate a mysterious animal in the form of a deer with eight legs. This phenomenon diverted the king's mind, and he pursued it. But alas! The deer, with its swift legs, quickly disappeared, drawing the King deep into the forest. At its disappearance, the King felt dejected and retraced his steps to find his companions. By then, he felt thirsty and hungry. He noticed at a distance a small hermitage made of mild leaves. He halted in front of it and, finding the door wide open, alighted from his horse and entered it. He could not find the owner of the hermitage. There was no temple there till then. But the sanctity of the place gained significant prominence. It was a dense mango forest where many sages, including Roma, Narada, Vaikhanasa, Dadhichi, Angeerasa, Jabali, Kalavar, Kanva, and others, were engaged in deep meditation and penance. But to his utter surprise, he found in a corner food and drink spread over a leaf as if offered to somebody. His acute thirst and hunger did not allow him to wait long. He unceremoniously helped himself to the food and drink. When he had finished the meal, he realized he was an intruder in the hermitage.
Sage Kusasanan, who had been to the river for his daily ablution, was entering the hermitage. The Rishi became angry and immediately cursed the intruder to turn into a dog for his canine actions, as only dogs sneakily creep into households and desecrate food. The intruder had not only desecrated the hermitage through his actions but had also violated the country's moral code. The curse became immediately effective, and the King turned into a roaming mongrel. Gunaseelan begged the Sage to take back his curse in place of his entire domain and wealth, but the words of the sage, who had already attained Vak Siddhi, were irrevocable. But seeing the humility, distress, and penitence of the King, Sage Kusasanan retorted to lighten the cruel rigor of the curse by saying that in due course of time, he would come across a holy place where he would regain his original form after a bath. In the form of a mongrel, the King had to roam around the earth, how long none could say. Once, during his wanderings, a juggler came before him and, finding him relatively healthy and plump, utilized his services to demonstrate sleight-of-hand tricks in the art of juggling.
Time passed, the mongrel in the company of the juggler roamed around the earth and, at last, reached Nanguneri. Before starting his show, the juggler took his bath in the temple tank and bathed the mongrel too. But to his surprise, the mongrel stood transformed as a king after the holy dip. People thronged around the juggler to see the wonderful jugglery of God. Such is the power of the holy waters of the sacred tank at Nanguneri.

*** The Vanamamalai Jeeyar Mutt headquarters are situated here at this kshethram. It is said that Manavaala Maamunigal used to preach here at this kshethram, and the Mutt was founded by Ponnadikaal Jeeyar, who was one among Manavaala Maamunigal’s eight sishyas.

It is said that Garuda and Adiseshan were once mortal enemies, engaging in a fierce battle due to the injustice committed by Adiseshan’s mother against Garuda’s mother. The story is as follows. Kadru ( Adiseshan’s mother) and Vinata ( Garudan’s mother) were both wives of Kashyapa Maharishi. One day, Kashyapa Maharishi asked his wives to ask him for a boon each. Kadru asked that she be blessed with a thousand sons. Vinata asked for two sons who would be brighter and stronger than all of Kadru’s sons combined. Thus, both Kadru and Vinata were blessed. Slowly, all of Kadru’s children were born. Five hundred years passed, but neither of Vinata’s eggs hatched into a  thousand nagas (snakes). In desperation, Vinata opened one of the eggs manually.
The offspring in the egg was still half-formed and, in anger at Vinata’s impatience, cursed her, saying she would become Kadru’s slave. But he also told her that in another five hundred years’ time, his brother would hatch, and he would be extremely powerful, and he would relieve Vinata of this curse. This offspring is known to us by the name of Arunan, the charioteer of Suryan. Even though he was half-formed, he had extreme tolerance and power. Hence, he was taken by Suryan as a charioteer. As time passed, the curse came into effect. One day, Kadru and Vinata were arguing about the color of Ucchaishravas' tail. Vinata claimed that the divine horse was a pure white color throughout, but Kadru said the horse’s body was white, but the tail was black. Thus, the two had a bet to see who was right. The one who would lose the bet would become the other’s slave. Kadru knew very well that the tail of Ucchaishravas was pure white, and knowing she would lose the bet, she told her sons to wrap themselves around the tail of Ucchaishravas so that she could win the bet. One day, in the presence of Kadru and Vinata, Ucchaishravas passed by with a black tail. Thus, Kadru won the bet, enslaving Vinata. For five hundred years, Vinata was a slave to Kadru. After five hundred years, Vinata’s second egg hatched, and from that egg was born Garudan. As soon as he was born, he went straight to his aunt and demanded that his mother be freed from slavery.
To this, Kadru put a condition, saying that if Garudan could bring the Amruthakalasham (the divine pitcher that contained the sacred nectar of immortality) for her and her children, she would release Vinata from slavery. Thus, Garudan immediately left for Swargalokam and defeated all the Devas in battle, successfully retrieving the Amruthakalasham. After retrieving the Amruthakalasham, Garudan returned to Bhulokam. On Bhulokam, Lord Vishnu was very impressed with Garudan for his strength and dedication. The Lord then offered Garudan a boon. Garudan asked that he should always be soaring far above the Lord; thus, Garudan is present in the Dwajasthambham outside the temple. The Lord also then told Garudan that he wanted Garudan to be constantly under his command, and thus asked Garudan to become his vaahanam. The Lord also relieved Vinata from slavery and returned the Amruthakalasham to the Devas.
In one of the battles between Garudan and Adiseshan, Adiseshan is said to have hidden in the pushkarani and performed tapas to the Lord to save him. Thus, the Lord appeared on the bank of the pushkarani and made Adiseshan his recliner. Hence, the Lord made sure that as long as He is present, both of His bhaktas do not fight amongst themselves.
It is said that if one prays to the Lord here, they will be relieved of all and any sarpa-dhosham.
***There is an interesting story that Vyagrapadar, who obtained a boon from Lord Shiva to possess the legs, hands, and eyes of a tiger, worshipped Lord Vishnu at this kshethram, and hence it gained the name Sirupuliyur.

Legend has it that Lord Shiva and Devi Parvati once engaged in a competition to determine who was the better dancer. When the world was asked, they all responded, saying Lord Shiva was the better dancer. In hopes of getting a second opinion, Devi Parvati suggests that the divine couple go to Vaikuntham and ask Lord Vishnu for his opinion, as His opinion was supreme, and nobody could question Him. When the question was put before the Lord, he said he would watch the divine couple dance and would decide then who among them was a better dancer. Thus, a mandapam was constructed by Vishvakarma, known as the Chitra Mandapam. The Lord descended from Vaikuntham along with Sridevi and Bhudevi reclining on Adiseshan. Lord Shiva appeared as Nataraja at the forefront of the Chitra Mandapam. All the devas and Lord Brahma descended to Bhulokam to witness the spectacle of Lord Nataraja and Devi Parvati’s dance. Thus, Lord Nataraja and Devi Parvati began dancing, and all those present to witness the spectacle watched in awe as the duo danced at a level never before seen. After the divine dance performance was concluded, Lord Vishnu asked everyone present at the event who they thought performed better. Everyone voted in favor of Lord Nataraja, and Lord Vishnu simply obliged by lifting his head. Devi Parvati, in anger, fled the scene and took the form of Devi Kali outside Chidambaram. Thus, one can still see a temple of Devi Kali here outside Chidambaram.

*** The Lord here is said to be a direct reincarnation of Tirumalai Srinivasa Perumal. The Lord here is reclining on the seven-headed serpent Adiseshan, whereas the Lord standing at Tirumalai is standing atop seven hills. Govindaraja Perumal is depicted with Shankam and Chakram, one hand supporting his head and the other hand displaying the Varada Mudra. Similarly, Srinivasa Perumal can be seen with Shankam, Chakram, one hand tucked inside and another hand showcasing Varada Mudra.
This temple has a rich history. During the Chola rule, Kulothunga Chola II was said to have uprooted the presiding idol of the Lord from the Shrine at the Nataraja temple to show Shaiva dominance. It is said that Bhagavat Ramanujacharya took the utsava moorthy (Paartasarathy Perumal) to Govindrajapatnam at Tirupati. When the kings changed over time, Krishnappa Nayaka of the Madurai Nayaka dynasty played a crucial role in reinstalling the Lord in this temple. There was considerable resistance from the Shaivaites present at Chidambaram at the time to reinstalling an idol of Lord Vishnu in a temple dedicated to Lord Shiva. However, the king remained unmoved and reinstated the idol of the Lord, as seen in modern times.

amongst them was a better dancer. Thus a mandapam was constructed by Vishvakarma

that was known as Chitra Mandapam. The Lord descended from Vaikuntham along with

Sridevi and Bhudevi reclining on Adiseshan. Lord Shiva appeared as Nataraja at the




forefront of the Chitra Mandapam. All the devas and Lord Brahma descended to Bhulokam

to witness the spectacle of Lord Nataraja and Devi Parvati’s dance. Thus Lord Nataraja and

Devi Parvati began dancing, and all who were present to witness the spectacle watched in

awe as the duo performed a dance at a level that was never before seen. After the divine

dance performance was concluded, Lord Vishnu asked everyone present at the event as to

who they thought performed better. Everyone voted in favor of Lord Nataraja, and Lord

Vishnu simply obliged by lifting his head. Devi Parvati, in anger, fled the scene and took the

form Devi Kali outside Chidambaram. Thus one can still see a temple of Devi Kali here

outside Chidambaram.

*** The Lord here is said to be a direct reincarnation of Tirumalai Srinivasa Perumal. The

Lord here is reclining on the seven-headed serpent Adiseshan whereas, the Lord standing

at Tirumalai is standing atop seven hills. Govindaraja Perumal can be seen with Shankam,

Chakram, one hand supporting His head and another hand showcasing the Varada Mudra.

Similarly, Srinivasa Perumal can be seen with Shankam, Chakram, one hand tucked inside

and another hand showcasing Varada Mudra.

This temple has been through a lot of history. During the Chola rule, Kulothunga Chola II

was said to have uprooted the presiding idol of the Lord from the Shrine at the Nataraja

temple to show Shaiva dominance. It is said that Bhagavat Ramanujacharya took the utsava

moorthy (Paartasarathy Perumal) to Govindrajapatnam at Tirupati. When the kings

changed over time, Krishnappa Nayak of the Madurai Nayak dynasty was instrumental in

reinstalling the Lord in this temple. There was a lot of resistance from the Shaivaites

present at Chidambaram at the time from reinstalling an idol of Lord Vishnu in a temple of





Lord Shiva. But the king was unmoved and reinstalled the idol of the Lord as it is seen in

the modern-day.

Legend has it that Lord Krishna built the city of Dwarka with the assistance of Vishwakarma. After Lord Krishna had killed Kansa, his two wives became widows. Kansa’s wives were the daughters of Jarasandha. Jarasandha swore to exact revenge against Lord Krishna, who had caused his daughters to suffer a cruel fate. Jarasandha attacked Mathura seventeen times. Each of these seventeen times, Lord Krishna defended Mathura. After all these attacks, Lord Krishna deemed that Mathura was no longer fit for stay as Jarasandha would continue to attack the state. Lord Krishna orders Vishwakarma to claim land from Samudraraja and convert it into a grand city that would be safe from any form of invasion. Thus, Dwarka came into being. Dwarka is among the Mukthi Kshethrams along with Ayodhya, Mathura, Maya (Haridwar), Kashi, Kanchipuram, and Avantika (Ujjain).
Apart from this divyadesam, there are four other Dwarkas. Together, the five kshethrams are collectively known as PanchaDwarka.
The five Dwarkas include:
Dwarka
Rukmini Dwarka
Beyt Dwarka
Dakor Dwarka
Shrinathji Dwarka


Rukmini Dwarka:
This kshethram is located 3.1 km from Dwarka. This Dwarka houses Rukmini Devi, whom Durvasa Maharishi cursed to stay away from Lord Krishna. Performing neer-daanam at this kshethram is of importance. Even the prasadam offered here is that of water

Beyt Dwarka:
This kshethram is located on an island off the coast of mainland India. To reach this kshetram, one must travel by boat from Okha Port or by road using the Sudarshana Setu. This kshethram was once connected to the mainland. It is said that after Lord Krishna left this world for Paramapadam, the land that connected the mainland to this kshethram was reclaimed by Samudraraja. This is the kshethram where Sudama visited the Lord to ask for alms. Sudama never asked for anything from the Lord, but he was presented with more than he could ever have asked for. It is said that Meerabai attained moksham here at this kshethram when she merged with the Lord.

Dakor Dwarka:
This kshethram is located near Anand in Gujarat. The Lord is called Ranchodraiji. It is said that in the seventeenth encounter with Jarasandha, the Lord started to run from the battlefield when He was faced against an asuran called Kaalayavanan. It is said that the Lord left the battlefield near Mathura and ran till the Junagadh district in modern-day Gujarat. Here, there was an ancient sooryavanshi king named Muchukunda who lay asleep after gaining a boon from Indra. There was once a great battle between the devas and the asuras. To win the battle, Indra took the help of Lord Ram’s ancestor, King Muchukunda. After winning the battle for the devas, Indra gave Muchukunda the boon that he could sleep for a long time to take a rest after the long and drawn-out battle. When Muchukunda would awake from this sleep, the first thing he would lay his eyes would turn into ash. Lord Krishna ran into the cave and awoke Muchukunda from his sleep in such a way that the first person he would lay his eyes on would be Kaalayavanan. When Kaalayavanan came in Muchukunda’s line of sight, he turned to ash. The idol of the Lord present at Dakor Dwarka is said to have originally been in Dwarka. After the idol was brought to Dakor, another idol that Devi Rukmini was worshiping was installed in the temple at Dwarka.

Shrinathji Dwarka:
This kshethram is located in Nathdwara, Rajasthan. This kshethram was established by Sri Vallabhacharya. The idol is said to have been installed in this temple by Meerabai. The idol is said to be a swayambhu moorthy, which is believed to have originated from the Govardhana Parvatham and became the object of worship in the Mevar Royal family, where Meerabai was born.

According to legend, it is said that during the Krita Yugam, two demons by the name Madhu and Kaitabha stole the Vedas from Lord Brahma and disappeared into the Pralaya Samudram (Ocean of Deluge). As seen at Tirucherai, Kaveri Devi was deemed greater than Ganga Devi. Hence, it is said that Ganga comes to this kshethram and bathes here in the Kaveri river to rid herself of her sins.

*** A peculiarity seen here with Lord is that he is seen in the Veera Shayanam. Anywhere one goes and sees the Lord in Shayana Kolam, one can see that the Lord will not be holding His shankam and chakram. However, here at this kshethram, as He carries His weapons and is in a reclined posture, He is said to be in the Veera Shayanam.

According to temple history, the Lord first appeared in the Satya Yuga. The first account of the Lord is mentioned in the Ramayana. As we know, the great King Dasharatha performed the Putrakameyishti Yagam to obtain children. The Putrakameyishti is a supplement to the Ashwamedha Yagna. It is said that Dasharatha first performed the Ashwamedha, and the origin of the Lord is believed to be found in this act. It is noted that Dasharatha asked his son-in-law, the sage Rishyashringa, to make arrangements to perform the Ashwamedha, where he recounts the story of an Ashwamedha Yagna performed by Lord Brahma. The story states that Lord Brahma once performed an Ashwamedha Yagna in a very sacred place that would yield a multifold increase in merit. In his research, he decided to perform this Yagna at a place known as Hasthigiri. It is said that he sat atop Hastigiri and prepared the sacrificial altar. According to Vaideeka Shastram, Goddess Saraswati had to accompany Lord Brahma to perform this Yagna. At this point, he was faced with two problems. The first being that Goddess Saraswati was not present, and the second being that there was no image of Lord Vishnu present at the sacrifice.  Lord Brahma decided to address the second problem first. To address this problem, Lord Brahma summoned Vishwakarma, the architect, and had him design an image of Lord Vishnu for the Devas. Lord Brahma wanted this idol to be useful for generations to come. He hence sought to make the idol of the Lord from a material whose properties would be beneficial to anyone who sought the Lord's blessings. Lord Brahma’s four heads signify each of the four Vedas. That is when Lord Brahma recollected that in the Atharvana Veda, there was a mention of a tree known as Udhumbara, which, when worshiped with devotion, has the power to annihilate any forces of enmity to the worshiper. So, what is Udumbara? Udumbara is a tree known as Ficus racemosa, which belongs to the fig family (athi tree). Brahma selected this tree because it offers numerous benefits, as per Ayurveda. Hence, Vishwakarma crafted the wood from the fig tree into a resplendent idol of the Lord. So the second problem was solved. To address the first problem, Lord Brahma decided to call upon his second wife, Goddess Savitri, to take Goddess Saraswati’s place. It is said that Goddess Saraswati had gotten into a tussle with Lord Brahma and had decided to seek solace to contemplate what had gone wrong. When Goddess Saraswati learned what Lord Brahma was doing, she became furious. In a fury, she decided that she wanted to destroy the sacrificial altar and hence put a stop to the Yagna in totality. It is said that the Goddess Saraswati took the form of a river known as Vegavathy and began to flow at a rapid speed towards the altar. Before Goddess Saraswati could reach the altar, she witnessed the idol of Athi Vardar and decided to flow beneath his feet as a mark of respect to her father-in-law. Thus the Yagna reached a conclusion. During the culmination of the Yagna, a resplendent Vimanam, known as the Punyakoti Vimanam, rose from the sacrificial altar. In the shade of this Vimanam stood a beautiful utsava moorthy of the Lord, known as Perarulaalan or Varadarajan. 
 

Modern Day
Around the 1520s, the Vijayanagara empire was the ruler of South India. They contributed immensely to the temple. One such contribution is the “Noor-Kaal Mandapam,” or a Hundred Pillared Mandapam, which Achyutha Deva Raya, the brother of the great Krishna Deva Raya, built. Around the 16th century, a significant shift occurred in the Delhi Sultanate when the Mughals gained control of North India and began expanding south. Towards the end of the Mughal Rule, when Aurangzeb took over, he began to plunder the temples and loot their wealth. The Vaishnavas of Kanchipuram sought to protect both the Moola Vigraham and the Utsava Moorthy from the invasion. To protect the Utsava Moorthy, the idol was carried by palanquin to a remote place called Udayarpalayam, where the local chief agreed to host and protect the Lord. Now, protecting the Moola Moorthy was a herculean task, as the idol was nearly 9 feet in length. Thus, a place had to be discovered where the Lord could be kept safe. The Vaishnavas then dug a giant pit within the temple tank (Ananthasaras) and embalmed Athi Varada, placing him alongside Adisesha to protect the Lord.
Over a while, the temple did not have a Moola Moorthy or a Utsava Moorthy. After Aurangzeb’s invasion, the temple was in ruins, with the Punyakoti Vimanam destroyed. Thus, the temple was reconstructed, but the daily rituals of the temple couldn’t be performed in the absence of the Lord. Hence, after major tussles with the chief of Udayarpalayam, the Utsava Moorthy was brought back to the temple. But the Moola Moorthy was lost as the people who had dug the pit were either very old or had passed away. Thus, the temple needed to install a Moola Moorthy in the temple. Hence, an idol of the Lord, known as Devaraja, found in a hamlet called Pazhayasheevaram, was brought to Kanchipuram and installed in the temple. Later, sometime in the 18th Century, when the temple tank was being cleaned, the idol of Athi Varada was found. At this time, the scholars came to the consensus that the idol would be preserved, and the idol of the Lord would be displayed for the devotees for 48 days, after which it would be returned to the temple tank to remain there for 40 years.

Over a while, the temple did not have a Moola Moorthy or an Utsava Moorthy. After

Aurangzeb’s invasion, the temple was in ruins, with the Punyakoti Vimanam totally

destroyed. Thus the temple was reconstructed, but the daily rituals of the temple couldn’t be

performed in the absence of the Lord. Hence after major tussles with the chief of

Udayarpalayam, the Utsava Moorthy was brought back to the temple. But the Moola Moorthy

was lost as the people who had dug the pit were either very old or had passed away. Thus

the temple needed to install a Moola Moorthy in the temple. Thus an idol of the Lord known

as Devaraja was found in a hamlet known as Pazhayasheevaram was brought to

Kanchipuram and installed in the temple. Later sometime in the 18th Century, when the



temple tank was being cleaned, the idol of Athi Varada was found. At this time, the scholars

came to the consensus that the idol will be preserved and the idol of the Lord shall grace the

devotees for 48 days, after which the idol shall be kept back in the temple tank to rise again

after 40 years.

During Samudra Manthanam, Mahalakshmi appeared from the Ksheerasagaram. Upon appearing, she was searching for Lord Vishnu so that she could be reunited with him once again. She sees the Lord but is embarrassed to put the Varamala around his neck as there were thirty-three crore gods(men) who were present there at the time. She thus decided to seek the Lord in private and went to Tirukanamangai, where she performed penance within the Darshana Pushkarani to bring the Lord there in solitude. The Lord appeared, and as Mahalakshmi was about to put the Varamala around the Lord’s neck, all the Devas appeared once more to witness the spectacle of the Lord’s marriage. The Lord thought that if the devas continued to stay in the form of men, Mahalakshmi would once again run away in embarrassment. Hence, he changed all the Devas into bees. As soon as this was done, Mahalakshmi married the Lord.

***Even today, outside the shrine of Abhishekavalli Thayaar, one can find a hive of bees buzzing around, symbolizing the presence of the Devas at the temple to date.

Brighu Maharshi, Gautama Rishi, and Brahma worshipped Lord Vishnu at this kshethram. It is also believed that Vasishtar created an image of Lord Krishna out of butter and meditated upon it. Lord Krishna is said to have appeared one day when Vasishtar was performing aaradhanam for the butter idol. When the Lord saw the butter idol, he was tempted and gobbled it up. When Vasishtar started to look for the butter idol, he saw a boy running away, saying he had eaten up the butter. Vasishtar began to chase the child. As the Lord was being chased by Vasishtar, a group of sages who were meditating under a Magizha tree caught sight of the boy, recognizing Him to be the Lord. The Lord is then said to have taken the form of Damodaran( the one who was tied up). Thus, this kshethram became the home of Lord Krishna. Hence the name Tirukkannankudi. 

Thirukannangudi Divyadesam and Thirumangai Azhwar

Once, when Thirumangai Azhwar was building the massive outer walls of the Srirangam temple, he ran out of money. To find a way, he went to the Buddhist Vihara at Nagapattinam. There, he sang a verse saying that for Buddha, it was enough to have a statue made of iron, wood, brass, or any simple metal—there was no need for it to be made of gold.

As he sang, something strange happened. The gold from the Buddha statue started to melt and flowed towards him, turning into gold bars. With that gold, he set off to Srirangam.

On the way, he became tired and rested under a tamarind tree. Before lying down, he buried the gold near the tree and told the tree to wake him up if anyone came by. The tree, taking his words seriously, stayed alert all night and didn’t “sleep.” That’s why it’s known as Urangaa Puli—the Tamarind Tree That Didn’t Sleep.

The next morning, a landlord from that area came by. The tree dropped a few leaves on Azhwar, waking him up just in time. Seeing the gold, the landlord claimed that since it was found on his land, it belonged to him. But Thirumangai Azhwar told him the land actually belonged to him and that he had the documents to prove it in Srirangam. He said he would go there, bring back the papers, and settle the matter. But he never came back. The issue was never resolved and is still said to be “pending.” That’s why it’s called Theraa Vilakku—the Case That’s Still Not Settled.

On the journey, Azhwar became very thirsty. He saw a few women near a well and asked them for some water. But since he had an argument with the landlord from their village, they refused to give him any. Angry at this, Azhwar cursed that the wells in that village would go dry forever. That’s why the place came to be called Oorak Kinaru—the Village of Dry Wells.

Tired, thirsty, and hungry, Thirumangai Azhwar lay down under a Maghizham Tree. The tree gently fanned him with its cool breeze and gave him some comfort. At that moment, Lord Parthasarathy (Paranthaman) appeared in the form of a Brahmin. He gave Azhwar some food and water. After eating, when Azhwar looked around, the Brahmin had disappeared. He then realized it was the Lord Himself. Feeling blessed and happy, he gave a boon to the tree that it would never dry up. From then, that tree has been called Kaaya Magizhai—the Maghizham Tree That Never Dries.

It is believed that Neelamegha Perumal vanquished a demon called Veekatakshan with His chakram, and hence the presiding deity is found with the prayoga chakram. It is also thought that the Lord in the sanctum miraculously showed the growth of hair to protect the words of a devout priest, Rangabhattar. It is said that the local king was visiting the temple on a given day, and Rangabhattar had already given the garland the Lord adorned to his lover. When the king arrived at the temple, there was no garland to perform the required honors. He requested the king to perform pradakshinam of the temple, by which time he would arrange for a garland. He sent a boy to fetch the garland from his lover. When the garland was presented to the king, he found a strand of hair in it. The king then questioned Rangabhattar as to where that hair had come from, to which Rangabhattar said the hair was that of the Lord’s. When the king came to examine the same in the morning, he found hair behind the crown that was placed atop the Lord’s head.  Hence, the Lord attained the name Sowrirajan.

The name of the kshethram is Tirukarambanur. This is because the Lord showed Himself to Maharishi Kadambha. Additionally, the Lord had taken the form of a Kadambha tree, to which Lord Brahma used to perform aaradhanam by pouring holy water from his kamandalam. Another story associated with this kshethram is similar to that of Tirukandiyoor. It is said that Lord Brahma once had five heads. In a rage, Lord Shiva once slapped Lord Brahma’s fifth head, as he also had five heads, and it stuck to his hand as a curse. The only way the Bramhakapalam falls from one’s hand is to beg for alms, and for that to fill up the kapalam. In his search for alms, Lord Shiva reached Karambanur. Here, when he begged Poornavalli thayaar for alms, the kapalam burst, and Lord Shiva was free of the curse. Thus, it is said that people without a means of obtaining food can come here to pray to Poornavalli Thayar to gain her blessings.
* This is said to be the only temple where one can see the Trinity with their wives all under the same temple. There are temples where one can see Lord Vishnu, Lord Brahma, and Lord Shiva together. However, this is the only temple where you will see Lord Vishnu with Poornavalli Thayaar (Lakshmi), Lord Brahma with Saraswati, and Lord Shiva with Parvati.

The legend recounts the story of how the Lord appeared at this kshetram as the Saptarishis performed tapas, with the intention of seeing the Lord in the form of Sri Nrisimha. The rishis requested a local ruler to protect them from the prevailing demons in the area while they performed the necessary yagnams to please the Lord. The king tried his best to keep the rishis safe, but was defeated after some time. At this point, Lord Rama had just defeated Ravana and was on his way back to rule Ayodhya. Thus, He instructed Hanuman to go and protect the rishis from all and any danger that was prevalent in the area. It is said that Hanuman held the Shankam and Chakram at this kshethram to protect the rishis from every possible risk. After successful completion of the tapas and yagnams, Lord Nrisimha emerged seated in padmasana as Yoga Nrisimha.
*** Another name of this kshethram is Gadikachalam, as Gadika means 24 minutes. It is said that if one spends 24 minutes at the top of the hill, it absolves all sins that one has committed throughout one's life. There are two hills at this kshethram: one large hill with 1,300 steps, which houses Sri Yoga Nrisimha Perumal, and a smaller hill with 750 steps, which houses Sri Yoga Anjaneya Perumal. This is the only place where one can see Anjaneyar with Shanku and Chakram seated in padmasana. Sri Anjaneyar faces Lord Nrisimha. It is said that Lord Nrisimha constantly blesses Lord Anjaneyar. It is said that if one visits both of these temples, they will never be plagued by any kind of ghosts, spirits, or ghouls of any kind.

Legend tells the story of Kubera losing all his wealth because he had inappropriately seen Devi Parvati. When he asked for Her forgiveness, Devi Parvati asked him to go to Tirukkolur and perform tapas towards Lord Vishnu, and he would regain his wealth. Thus, Kubera is said to have come to this kshethram, and after performing tapas, the Lord appeared as Vaithamanidi Perumal, who brought all of Kubera’s wealth. The Lord is said to have kept Kubera’s wealth under Adisesha and slept over it. Thus, Kubera received their kripa-kataksham in the form of keeping his wealth safe and also gaining interest over time. The Lord’s left-hand houses kajal. The Lord is said to be looking at this hand to find more wealth for Kubera’s treasury.
Another story tells the tale of pralaya-kalam. Dharma is said to have taken a human form and prostrated at the Lord’s feet to fight against adharma. The Lord is said to establish dharma by defeating all factors causing adharma at the time.

*** This kshethram is the avatara sthalam of Madhurakavi Azhwar.

It is said that Ambareesha was such an ardent devotee that the Sudharshana Chakra had made himself self-obligated to rush for Ambareesha’s protection. One day, the great sage Durvasa decided to pay a visit to Ambareesha. Ambareesha had undertaken the Dwadashi-Vratam, in which one must break the fast after Ekadashi and feed their people at the start of Dwadashi. Durvasa Maharishi told Ambareesha that he would take a bath and then join him in the Dwadashi-Vratam. Ambareesha agreed to wait for Durvasa Maharishi. Hours went by, but Durvasa Maharishi was nowhere to be seen. On the advice of Sage Vasishta, Ambareesha broke his fast by taking holy water. At this moment, Durvasa Maharishi arrived and, in his temper, threw a lock of his hair to the ground. This hair grew into a monstrous demon that chased Ambareesha to devour him. At this moment, the Sudharshana Chakra of the Lord came to Ambareesha’s rescue and cut the demon into tiny pieces. Further, the Chakra started to chase after Durvasa Maharishi. Durvasa Maharishi began to run and sought refuge with Lord Brahma, Lord Shiva, and ultimately at the heavenly abode of Lord Vishnu himself. Still, the Chakra continued to pursue Durvasa Maharishi. Lord Vishnu instructed Durvasa Maharishi to go and fall at Ambareesha’s feet and ask for his forgiveness. Durvasa Maharishi then falls at Ambareesha’s feet for his forgiveness. Ambareesha forgives Durvasa Maharishi, and the Sudharshana Chakra stops going after Durvasa Maharishi. It is said that 
Ambareesha used to pray to this Lord, and with this Lord’s grace, he was protected.

The legend has it that the Devas came together (goshti) to worship the Lord at this kshetram to rid the universe of the demon Hiranyakashipu. This temple is also considered Dakshina Badri. This is probably the most important kshetrham according to the Sri Vaishnava Parampara, as it is the kshetram where Swami Bhagawad Ramanujar first performed the Ashtakshara Mantropadesham. Let us see the story. Swami Ramanujar came here to this kshethram to seek education from Sri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal. Sri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal is said to have rejected giving Swami Ramanujar education seventeen times, sending him back to Sri Rangam. When Swami Ramanujar came back for the eighteenth time, Sri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal is said to have revealed the ashtakshara mantram and the charama shlokam to Swami Ramanujar and instructed him to keep it a secret. Swami Ramanujar realized that this mantram and shloka were the means to Sri Vaikuntham. Thus, Swami Ramanujar is said to have climbed up to the top of the Ashtanga Vimanam and openly revealed that he possessed the ashtakshara mantram as well as the charama shlokam and was willing to pass it on to anyone who so wished to listen to him. When Sri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal learned of this, he immediately pursued Swami Ramanujar. He told him that he was destined to go to hell because he had not listened to his guru’s wishes. Swami Ramanujar is then supposed to have said that he was more than ready to go to hell if he could provide the means for so many people to go to Vaikuntham. Sri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal then realizes his mistake and is said to have asked for forgiveness of Swami Ramanujar after seeing his broad outlook.

Ashtanga Vimanam with the arch from where Swami Ramnujar performed mantropadesham

It is said that the Lord is said to have taken this form when asked by Mrugandu Maharishi asked to see the Lord as Trivikramar. The Lord present here is an exact mirror image of the Lord standing at Tirukazhicheerama Vinnagaram. One peculiarity of the Lord standing here is that the Lord is holding the Shankam in the right hand and the Chakram in the left hand.

The first three of the Azhvars — Poigai Azhwar, Bhoothath Azhwar, and Pey Azhwar — came to Thirukkovilur on a rainy night. First to arrive was Poigai Azhwar, from Kanchipuram, who sought refuge for the night at the ashram of Mrugandu Rishi. The rishi told him that there was a place for just one person to sleep and that he was welcome to stay for the night.
Bhoothath Azhwar, from Mamallapuram, followed shortly, and he too requested that he stay at the ashram for the night. PoigaiAzhwar welcomed him, saying there was a place for one to sleep and two to sit, and took him inside.
Pey Azhwar, from Mylapore, too, reached the ashram. He was told that there was a place for one to sleep, two to sit, and three to stand. It is explained as a slogan by
“Oruvar Padukka – Iruvar Irukka – Moovar Nirkalam”.
 The three of them stood there through the night, sharing their experiences with each other.
A little later, the three Azhwars sensed the presence of a fourth person, and with space only for three to stand, they felt uncomfortable. Through their exceptional vision, the three Azhwars realized that the fourth person was none other than Lord Vishnu himself. Delighted at this, they showered praises on the Lord.
This is the first temple where the first three Azhwars sang praises (Pasurams) of Lord Vishnu, the compilation of which later came to be known as the Naalayira Divya Prabhandham.
It is believed that this ashram, where the 3 Azhwars stayed that rainy night, is the one where one, today, finds the sanctum. The first of the three Azhwars also finds a place inside the Sanctum.

There was once a Chozha king by the name Dharmavarman who lived in Kumbakonam. Once, when the king had gone on a hunting trip, he found that a few rishis were distressed by the attack of demons and sought the king's help to kill them. The king bravely defended the rishis and stayed in the forest for some time to look after the welfare of the rishis. At this time, the king was saddened by his inability to father any children. The rishis then performed a yajna to help the king in his time of difficulty. As the rishis were performing the yajna, a voice boomed from the sky, stating that if the king wanted children, he must pray to Goddess Lakshmi. Thus, the king prayed to Goddess Lakshmi. One day, as he was going through the forest, he noticed a very peculiar lotus blooming in a pond. Upon further inspection, he saw that the lotus had a thousand petals, and in the center, a beautiful baby girl was nestled. Goddess Lakshmi had answered the king’s prayers by reincarnating herself as the baby girl. As she was found in a lotus, Dharmavarman named the child Kamalavalli.
Here, the meaning of Kamala can be interpreted as Ka meaning Paramathma, Ma meaning the Jeevathma, and La meaning the one who helps reach. Therefore, Kamala means she who leads the Jeevathma to the Paramathma to attain moksham. Soon, a time came when Dharmavarman began to seek a suitor for Kamalavalli. Among the men in the swayamwaram, Lord Ranganathar of Sri Rangam was present. Seeing the Lord, Kamalavalli immediately garlanded the Lord. The Lord then left a form of Himself in the form of Sri Azhagiya Manavalan there in his stead. Thus, all the people gathered at the event witnessed the grand spectacle of the wedding of the Lord with Goddess Lakshmi.
During the Panguni Brahmotsavam in Sri Rangam, on the sixth day, the Lord travels to Urayur to marry Sri Lakshmi. Thus, between the two kshethrams, there is only one utsava moorthy. This kshethram does not conduct Brahmotsavam on its own.

The rishis, headed by Kashyapa, began to perform a sacrifice on the banks of the Ganga. Sage Narada visited them and asked them why they were performing the sacrifice and who would be pleased by it. Unable to answer the question, the rishis approached Sage Bhrigu to find a solution through direct ascertainment of reality.
Bhrigu first went to Satyalokam, the abode of Lord Brahma. At Satylokam, he found Lord Brahma reciting the four Vedas in praise of Lord Narayana, with each of his four heads, and attended upon by Saraswati. Lord Brahma did not take notice of Bhrigu offering obeisance. Concluding that Lord Brahma was unfit for worship, Bhrigu left Satyalokam for Kailasham, the abode of Lord Shiva.
At Kailasham, Bhrigu found Lord Shiva spending his time pleasantly with Parvati, unaware of his presence. Parvati drew Shiva's attention to the presence of the sage. Lord Shiva was furious at Bhrigu’s intrusion and tried to destroy him. The sage cursed Lord Shiva and left for Vaikuntam. At Vaikuntam, Lord Vishnu was reposing on Adisesha with Sri Mahalakshmi in service at His feet. Finding that Sriman Narayana also did not notice him, the sage became infuriated and kicked the Lord on his chest, the place where Mahalakshmi resides.
At once, Lord Vishnu hastened to apologize to the angry sage and pressed his feet to allay the pain caused to Bhrigu’s leg. In doing so, the Lord removed the eye in the foot of the sage, which gave Bhrigu power to defy the Devas. Thereupon, the sage decided that Lord Vishnu was the most supreme of the Trimurtis and informed the rishis accordingly. Thereupon, they decided that Lord Vishnu was the fruit of the yaga. Sri Mahalakshmi was angered by the action of her Lord in apologizing to Bhrigu, who committed an offense. She, therefore, left Vaikuntam without heeding the entreaties of the Lord. She furiously ran to Kolhapur and began to perform tapas to get the Lord’s attention once more. At the same time, the Lord had taken the form of Sri Srinivasa and was marrying Devi Padmavathi. When Mahalakshmi found out what was happening, she rushed to take her anger out on the Lord. The Lord is said to have run to Kumbakonam and hidden in the temple as Pathala Srinivasar. Mahalakshmi was determined to be reunited with the Lord; thus, she stayed in Kumbakonam and performed tapas to fulfill her desires. 
At around the same time, Brighu Maharishi had reincarnated as Hema Maharishi and was residing in Kumbakonam. One day, in the temple, a pushkarani found a baby girl among thousands of lotus flowers blooming in the tank. Hema Maharishi realized that this child was none other than the incarnation of Mahalakshmi and decided to adopt her. As she came of age, She desired to get married to the Lord. During Makara Sankranthi, the Lord descended from Sri Vaikuntham in a grand chariot, and after marrying Komalavalli, Thayaar stayed in Kumbakonam along with his chariot. Even today, when we visit this temple, we can see that the garbha griha features a grand chariot in which the Lord is reclining in the Udyoga Shayanam posture.
 Udyoga Shayanam is a peculiar posture, as the Lord is neither completely asleep nor completely upright. It is said that Tirumahisai Azhwar was once having a conversation with the Lord. The Lord then was about to get up to greet Tirumahisai Azhwar when he told the Lord that he looked notably different and lovely in that position. Hence, the Lord is said to have permanently taken that posture.
***This kshethram is credited for the resurfacing of the Naalayira Divyaprabandhangal (compilation of all the Azhwar Pasurams).  At one point, all of the Naalayira Divyaprabandhangal were lost except for ten Pasurams that were being sung at this temple. Here, Naathamunigal heard this, and the verses told ten out of a thousand Pasurams. This had Naathamunigal intrigued as to where the other nine hundred and ninety Pasurams had disappeared. These ten Pasurams also spoke of Kurugur (present-day Azhwar Tirunagari) and Sadagopan (Nam Azhwar). Thus Naathamunigal went in search of Nam Azhwar. Upon reaching Kurugur and inquiring about these ten Pasurams, the locals denied knowing of the ten Pasurams he had asked for, but they were familiar with eleven other Pasurams. Naathamunigal recited these eleven Pasurams twelve thousand times in front of the divine tamarind tree where Nam Azhwar had once resided. Upon completion of the recitation, Nam Azhwar is said to have appeared in front of Naathamunigal and blessed him with the thousand Pasurams sung by him as well as the three thousand other Pasurams which were sung by the nine other Azhwars.
