attended upon by Saraswati. Lord Brahma did not take notice of Bhrigu offering obeisance.

Concluding that Lord Brahma was unfit for worship, Bhrigu left Satyalokam for Kailasham,

the abode of Lord Shiva.

At Kailasham, Bhrigu found Lord Shiva spending his time pleasantly with Parvati and not

noticing his presence. Parvati drew the attention of Shiva to the presence of the sage. Lord

Shiva was furious at Bhrigu’s intrusion and tried to destroy him. The sage cursed Lord Shiva

and left for Vaikuntam. At Vaikuntam, Lord Vishnu was reposing on Adisesha with Sri

Mahalakshmi in service at His feet. Finding that Sriman Narayana also did not notice him, the

sage was infuriated, and he kicked the Lord on His chest, the place where Mahalakshmi

resides.

At once, Lord Vishnu hastened to apologize to the angry sage and pressed his feet to allay the

pain caused to Bhrigu’s leg. In doing so, the Lord removed the eye in the foot of the sage,

which gave Bhrigu power to defy the Devas. Thereupon, the sage decided that Lord Vishnu

was the most supreme of the trimurthis and told the rishis the same. Thereupon, they



decided that Lord Vishnu was the fruit of the yaga. Sri Mahalakshmi was angered by the

action of her Lord in apologizing to Bhrigu, who committed an offense. She, therefore, left

Vaikuntam without heeding the entreaties of the Lord. She furiously ran to Kolhapur and

began to perform tapas to get the Lord’s attention once more. At the same time, the Lord had

taken the form of Sri Srinivasa and was getting married to Devi Padmavathi. When

Mahalakshmi found out what was happening, she rushed to take her anger out on the Lord.

The Lord is said to have run to Kumbakonam and hidden in the temple as Pathala Srinivasar.

Mahalakshmi was determined to be reunited with the Lord; thus, she stayed in Kumbakonam

and performed tapas to have her desires fulfilled.

At around the same time, Brighu Maharshi had reincarnated as Hema Maharishi and was

residing in Kumbakonam, and one day in the temple, pushkarani found a baby girl among

thousands of lotus flowers that were blooming in the tank. Hema Maharishi realized that this

child was none other than the incarnation of Mahalakshmi and decided to adopt her. As she

came of age, She desired to get married to the Lord. During Makara Sankranthi, the Lord

descended from Sri Vaikuntham in a grand chariot, and after getting married to Komalavalli,

Thayaar stayed in Kumbakonam along with his chariot. Even today, when we visit this

temple, we can see that the garbha griha consists of this grand chariot in which the Lord is

reclining in the Udyoga Shayanam.

Udyoga Shayanam is a very peculiar posture as the Lord is not completely asleep, nor is he

completely upright. It is said that Tirumahisai Azhwar was once having a conversation with

the Lord. The Lord then was about to get up to greet Tirumahisai Azhwar when he said the

Lord was looking particularly different and nice in that position. Hence the Lord is said to

have permanently taken that posture.



***This kshethram is credited for the resurfacing of the Naalayira Divyaprabandhangal

(compilation of all the Azhwar pashurams). At one point, all of the Naalayira

Divyaprabandhangal were lost except for ten pashurams that were being sung at this temple.

Here, Naathamunigal heard this, and the verses told ten out of a thousand pashurams. This

had Naathamunigal intrigued as to where the other nine hundred and ninety pashurams had

disappeared. These ten pashurams also spoke of Kurugur(present-day Azhwar Tirunagari)

Sadagopan(NamAzhwar). Thus Naathamunigal went in search of NamAzhwar. Upon

reaching Kurugur and enquiring about these ten pashurams, the locals denied knowing of

the ten pashurams that he asked for, but they knew of eleven other pashurams.

Naathamunigal recited these eleven pashurams twelve thousand times in front of the divine

tamarind tree where NamAzhwar had once resided. Upon completion of the recitation,

NamAzhwar is said to have appeared in front of Naathamunigal and blessed him with the

thousand pashurams sung by him as well as the three thousand other pashurams which were

sung by the nine other Azhwars.

Legend says that this Lord is extremely ancient and is said to have appeared before the appearance of Lord Brahma. When Lord Brahma is said to have appeared and become conscious of the Lord, acknowledging Him is said to have asked for a place to establish His idol and perform tapas. The Lord is said to have directed Lord Brahma to Kurugur by giving him the command of tapas kuru. As the Lord commanded Lord Brahma to perform tapas, this kshethram gained the name of Kurugur. Lord Brahma is said to have bathed in the Tamaraparani River and performed tapas. The Lord is said to have emerged as a Swayambhu Moorthy ( self-established and not carved by anyone ). Lord Brahma is said to have performed the prathishtapana of the Lord. Another legend tells the story that Indra was absolved of the curse given by his parents by praying to the Lord at this kshethram. It is believed that Lakshmi meditated on Lord Vishnu when He was on a vow of celibacy. In response to Her request, He accepted Her in marriage in the form of a garland of flowers (Magizha malar maalai).
***

Swami Nam Azhwar

This kshethram is said to be the avatara sthalam of Nam Azhwar. As we saw in Tirukurungudi, Nam Azhwar’s parents prayed to Kurungudi Nambi for a child who would be like the Lord Himself. It is said that Kurungudi Nambi Himself reincarnated as Nam Azhwar. We shall now see the story of Nam Azhwar, one of the most revered gurus in the Sri Vaishnava Parampara.
Forty-three days had passed since Lord Sri Krishna had ascended to Sri Vaikuntham. A childless couple, Kari and Udayanangai, visited Tirukurungudi to pray for the birth of a child. It is said that they prayed to the Lord for a child who would be like Him. As none in this universe is comparable to Him, it is noted that Nambi Himself reincarnated as Nam Azhwar. Thus, in the Vaikasi month, under Visakha, Nakshatram, Nam Azhwar was born. As soon as he was born, he exhibited very peculiar behavior in the form of not crying or suckling. The couple, out of concern, is said to have taken the baby to the Adinatha Perumal Temple to pray to the Lord for the baby’s well-being. Nam Azhwar is also said to be an amshavataram of Sri  Vishwakshenar, who is said to be third in line in the Acharya Parampara after the Lord Sriman Narayana and Mahalakshmi Thayaar. The couple is said to have tied a cradle near the Tamarind tree that was present in the temple courtyard.

Divine Tamarind Tree

The baby is said to have crawled out of the cradle and into a small, crater-like space within the tree, where it started a deep meditation. The baby is said to have stayed in this meditative state for sixteen years. At this time, Madurakavi Azhwar is said to have been at Ayodhya and offering argyam as per his Nityakarmam when he saw a blinding light at the edge of the horizon. Recognizing the meditative nature of the divine light is said to have started to follow the light. In pursuit of the light, Madurakavi Azhwar is said to have traveled south, crossing Tiruvenkatam, then Tiruvallikeni, then Sri Rangam, then Madurai, and finally reaching Kurugur. When Madurakavi Azhwar reached the divine tree, he saw a child in a deep meditative state and was worried if the child was still alive or not. Madurakavi Azhwar is said to have thrown a rock near the boy to test his consciousness. When the boy opened his eyes, Madurakavi Azhwar is said to have asked a question: “Sethathin Vayatrill Siriyadhu Pirandhaal Yeththai Thindru Enge Kiddakum?“. Madurakavi Azhwar was referring to the Jeevaathma. Madurakavi Azhwar asked, "When the jeevaathma enters a lifeless body, how would it survive, what would it feed on, and how would it sustain itself?" This is when Nam Azhwar is said to have first spoken by saying, “Aththaith Thindru Ange Kidakkum.”. Nam Azhwar’s reply said that the lifeless body would experience the pleasures and pains of life before attaining paramapadam or moksham. Madurakavi Azhwar was so stunned by the boy’s response that he begged to be his disciple. Madurakavi Azhwar composed 11 Pasurams in praise of his Acharya, Swami Nam Azhwar, known as Kanninun Shiruthambu, which are included among the 4000 Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
When Nam Azhwar was ready to attain paramapadam, Madurakavi Azhwar asked Nam Azhwar with full of tears, what to do next. Nam Azhwar advised Madurakavi Azhwar to boil the waters of Tamraparni, and he said that an idol would form during the boiling of the water. Madurakavi Azhwar followed Nam Azhwar’s advice. When he had boiled the waters of Tamraparni, He got an idol of Bhagavad Ramanuja. He was surprised to see that the idol was different from what he had expected. He went to Nam Azhwar with the idol, and the latter told him that this idol was that of a Bhavishyadhacharya (Future Acharya) and that he would be born 4000 years from then. He again advised boiling the waters of Tamraparni. Madurakavi Azhwar once again boiled the waters of Tamraparni and finally got the idol of Nam Azhwar.
Every year on the Tirunakashthram of Nam Azhwar, the NavaTirupati Brahmotsavam is concluded, and the teerthavaari uthsavam is performed where the idol of Nam Azhwar is brought to the Tamaraparani River, and along with Sri Sudharshana ChakrathAzhwar, Nam Azhwar’s Idol is also dipped in the holy waters of the river.

King Rukmangathan of the Suryavamsam is said to have offered flowers to the Lord daily as a form of kainkaryam. One day, the Devas saw the flowers and thought they were to be worshipped first by those beautiful flowers, and hence started to steal the flowers, making garlands for themselves and adorning themselves with them. One day, the king performed a yagam to reveal who was stealing the flowers. The king added numerous medicinal herbs to the divine flames of the yagnam, which released a cloud of smoke that revealed the devas wearing floral garlands. The king told the devas that if they had asked for the flowers, he would have given them the flowers without any second thought. The king said to the devas that they could take the flowers at any time and asked them to return to Amaravati(Devalokam). The devas informed the king that they were unable to return, as their powers had been rendered useless by the divine smoke emanating from the yagnam. The devas told the king that the only way they could return to Amaravati was if someone in the kingdom who was observing Ekadasi-vratham with a staunch following, without deviating from any of the rules, gave away the punyam that they gained by following the vratham. The king went searching throughout his kingdom and found a woman who was the only one in the entire kingdom who was religiously following the norms of the vratham.
The king explained the situation to her, and she gifted away all her punyam to the Devas, enabling them to reach Devalokam.

***There are also shrines for Krishna and Narasimhar.

This kshethram shares many aspects of its Sthala Puranam with that of Srivilliputtur. We will see the story of Periya Azhwar once again.
Periya Azhwar ( Vishnuchittar ) used to live in Srivilliputtur, leading a straightforward lifestyle, performing pushpa-kainkaryam to Sri Vatapatrashayee. During that time, there was a king named Vallabhadevan, whose capital was situated in Madurai. He was an ardent devotee of Lord Vishnu and wished to learn the meaning of the Vedas and Upanishads. He enquired with his chief minister as to how he could achieve this goal. The minister suggested that the king call all the Vedic Scholars present in his kingdom to debate and question all the matters present in the Vedas and Upanishads. The one who could solve all the questions posed by the king would be rewarded dearly. The king agreed with the minister’s suggestion, and soon an announcement was made throughout the kingdom saying there would be a grand meeting of all the Vedic Scholars in the land. The scholar who would impress the king with their answers would be rewarded with gold coins, which would be hung in a divine binding. The coins would present themselves to the person who would aptly answer all of the king’s questions. Many scholars came before the king, but none gave satisfactory answers that the king desired. One night, Lord Vatapatrashayee appeared in Vishnuchittar‘s dreams and instructed him to go to the king’s court to claim the prize that was being offered. Vishnuchittar told the Lord that he knew nothing about the Vedas or Upanishads. All he knew to do was to make garlands and present them to the Lord. The Lord then told Vishnuchittar not to worry and to go to the court. The Lord said He would speak through the mouth of Vishnuchittar. That same night, the Lord also appeared in the dreams of the chief minister and asked him to make royal arrangements to receive Vishnuchittar and escort him to the king’s court. 

The next morning, a royal elephant with palanquins arrived and carried Vishnuchittar to the royal court. As he entered, all the scholars began to murmur and pass sarcastic comments about him, knowing that his knowledge was limited. Vishnuchittar prostrated himself before the king and the gathered scholars, and then began his speech on the Vedas and Upanishads. As and when the king questioned, it was almost as though the answer to the question was pre-prepared and ready. Finally, to close his speech, Vishnuchittar made a final statement that said, “Sriman Narayanane Paramporul.” This translates to “It is Lord Sriman Narayana who is the only protector, and it is with His blessing that the universe is surviving. It is He and only He who is the underlying principle that is mentioned in the four Vedas and Upanishads. When this statement was made, the binding came undone, and the gold coins showered into Vishnuchittar‘s hands from above. The king was overcome with joy and ecstasy. All the gathered scholars lowered their heads in shame. The king then asked Vishnuchittar how he had spoken about all the Vedas and Upanishads in such simple language. Vishnuchittar then told the king that truly it was he who had spoken and that the Lord himself intended for this to perspire. The king was deeply moved by what Vishnuchittar said and fell to his feet. He arranged for complete royal honors and sent him around the kingdom in a royal procession. At one point, when Vishnuchittar looked up at the sky, he saw the Lord along with Mahalakshmi seated atop Garudan, granting their blessing to him. It was at that moment that, with eyes filled with tears of joy, he said the words, “Pallaandu, pallaandu pallayiratthandu palakodi noorayiram.” These words are still sung to date during sathumorai seva every day, whether it may be at a temple or within a household. 
*** One of the peculiarities observed in this temple is the presence of a Navagraha Sannidhanam. Usually, one does not observe Navagraha Sannidhanam in a Sri Vaishnava temple.
Another specialty of this temple is the Ashtanga Vimanam. It is one of the few temples in the country built in tiers. One can climb up and take a closer look at the Ashtanga Vimanam, which enshrines Pallikonda Perumal in one of its levels, and Surya Narayanan in a standing posture in the other. This aspect of a vimanam, consisting of three tiers enshrining three different postures of Lord Vishnu — sitting, standing, and reclining — is unique in South Indian temple architecture. The shadow of the Vimanam never falls on the ground.

the answer to the question was pre-prepared and ready. Finally, to close his speech,

Vishnuchittar made a final statement that said, “Sriman Narayanane Paramporul.” This

translates to “It is Lord Sriman Narayana who is the only protector, and it is with His

blessing that the universe is surviving. It is Him and only Him who is the underlying



principle that is mentioned in the four Vedas and Upanishads.”. When this statement was

made, the binding came undone, and the gold coins showered into Vishnuchittar‘s hands

from above. The king was overcome with joy and ecstasy. All the gathered scholars lowered

their heads in shame. The king then asked Vishnuchittar how he spoke about all the Vedas

and Upanishads in such a simple language. Vishnuchittar then told the king that truly it was

he who had spoken and that the Lord himself intended for this to perspire. The king was

deeply moved by what Vishnuchittar said and fell to his feet. He arranged for complete

royal honors and sent him around the kingdom in a royal procession. At one point,

when Vishnuchittar looked up at the sky, he saw the Lord along with Mahalakshmi seated

atop Garudan, granting their blessing to him. It was at that moment that with eyes filled

with tears of joy did he say the words“pallaandu, pallaandu pallayiratthandu palakodi

noorayiram.” These words are still sung to date during sathumorai seva every day, whether

it may be at a temple or within a household.


*** One of the peculiarities observed in this temple is the presence of a Navagraha

Sannidhanam. Usually, one does not observe Navagraha Sannidhanam in a Sri Vaishnava

temple.

Another specialty of this temple is the Ashtanga Vimanam. It is one of the few temples in

the country built in tiers. One can climb up and take a closer look at the Ashtanga Vimanam,

which enshrines Pallikonda Perumal in one of its levels, and Surya Narayanan in a standing

posture in the other. This aspect of a vimanam consisting of 3 tiers enshrining three

different postures of Lord Vishnu. in the sitting, standing, and reclining postures is quite

unique in the South Indian temple architecture. The shadow of the Vimanam never falls on

the ground.

The Sthala Puranam of this kshethram is found in Varaha Puranam. It is known as Kaisika Maahathmiyam.
Kaisika Ekadesi is celebrated in the Tamil Month of Kaarthigai on the succeeding Ekadesi in the Sukla Paksham. This is named after the Kaisika Puranam, which is the 48th Chapter in the Sri Varaha Puranam. The message behind the day reinforces the fact that caste is not a hindrance in attaining the lotus feet of Sriman Narayana, and true Bhakti alone is enough. This story took place in the Divyadesam of Thirukurungudi, one of the Nava Tirupati in Thirunelveli. Nambaduvaan was born in a low chandala kulam but was a devotee of Sriman Narayana. On every Ekadasi, he observed Vratham, sleeping not a single night, singing the glory of the Lord, and thinking about Him. On one Karthigai Ekadasi, Nambaduvaan left for the Kurungudi Nambi temple to observe his fast and recite some Pasurams using various Paan on Sri Kurungudi Nambi.On his way, Nampaduvan was confronted by a Brahma Rakshas. This Rakshas, who has been starved of food, tells Nampaaduvaan that he would devour him. Nampaduvan humbly requests that he has the duty of nama sankeerthanam. Nampaduvan pleads with the rakshas that he would return after his vratham and darshan of Kurungudi Nambi. He promises that he would indeed return; he mentions the various sins that he would incur if he were not to return. But for none of Nampaduvan’s promises, BrahmaRakshas was not satisfied. At last, Nambaduvaan promised that “Whoever thinks/says that Supreme Lord Sriman Narayanan is equivalent/on par with or inferior to other devathas, that paaapam would catch me!” After hearing this, Brahma Rakshas was moved and impressed by such a firm promise and said, 'Now I believe in you; you can go now and return soon.' I will wait for you till your return.” Nambaduvaan happily went to Sri Kurungudi temple, observed his jakratha vratham, and completed his vratham with singular determination. He returned as stated to BrahmaRakshas. Nampaduvan went and offered himself to the Rakshas. But his hunger had vanished, and instead, he was moved by the truthfulness of the Vishnu devotee. The Brahma Rakshas then told his story – he was a Brahmin who had been cursed to become a Brahma Rakshas by his elders because he had not performed the yajnas carefully. The Rakshas then asked Nampaduvan to give the reward of one of his prayers so that he could get liberation. Hearing the pleas of the BrahmaRakshas, Nambaduvan said that he never sang for any palam. However, he will still request Thirukurungudi Nambi to absolve the BrahmaRakshas of his sins. Nambi gives the palam of the last pasuram and relieves BrahmaRakshas of its sins. This story strongly reiterates that true Bhakti is sufficient to attain Him, and a person's caste is entirely insignificant. It is believed that those who read or listen to ‘Kaisika Purana’ on that day will be showered with the Lord’s abundant mercy! The story of Nampaduvan is narrated and acted in Vishnu Temples in South India on the Kaisika Ekadasi. Sri Parasara Bhattar chanted the Kaisika Puranam before Lord Ranganatha, and this tradition continues to date with the descendants of Bhattar chanting the puranam on Kaisika Dwadashi day at Srirangam each year. Kaisika Ekadasi is considered even more significant to Vaishnavas than Vaikunta Ekadasi, as it implies the steadfast Bhakti towards Sriman Narayana and His abundant mercy on His devotees.


Vaishnava Nambi Temple



Thirukurungudi Sri Vaishnava Nambi Dhivya Sevai in Kaisika Mandapam

This kshethram is one of the most important of all the Divyadesams. 
The following summarizes the importance of this kshethram:
1) It is said that Swami Bhagawad Ramanujacharya wanted uniformity in the way rituals were conducted throughout South India. To achieve this, he is said to have traveled to Tiruvananthapuram to plead with the Nambudri priests to follow practices as per the Pancharatra Agama Shastras. It is said that the Nambudri priests pleaded with Ananthapadmanabha Swamy to allow their prevailing traditions, which were being followed, to continue throughout Kerala. It is said that in the middle of the night, when Bhagawad Ramanujacharya was asleep, Kurungudi Nambi Swamy is said to have brought Bhagawad Ramanujacharya here to this kshethram. When Bhagawad Ramanujacharya awoke in the morning, he is said to have had a conversation with the Lord. The Lord tells Bhagawad Ramanujacharya that he has accomplished what He could not achieve in all His births. The Lord asks to be initiated into Sri Vaishnavism by Bhagawad Ramanujacharya. Bhagawad Ramanujacharya is said to have performed the Pancha-Samskara for the Lord here, thereby bestowing upon Him the name Sri Vaishnava Nambi.
2) It is said that Nam Azhwar’s parents came to this kshetram to pray for the birth of a child. The Lord is said to have had a conversation with Nam Azhwar’s parents, asking them what kind of child they desired. The parents are said to have asked for a child who is just like the Lord Himself. As none in this universe is like the Lord, it is said that the Lord Himself incarnated as Nam Azhwar.
3) This is the kshethram where Tirumangai Azhwar attained Paramapadam. There is a shrine here for Tirumangai Azhwar.

Mahendragiri

There is a mention of this kshethram in the Ramayana. It is said that Hanuman jumped from Mahendragiri Parvatham to fly to Sri Lanka in search of Sita, the wife of Lord Rama. Mahendragiri Parvatham is located within this kshethram. This is also the site of the Malai Mel Nambi Temple.

Legend has it that Yama, the lord of death, once undertook a pilgrimage. While visiting all the holy shrines, he was drawn to the serenity and beauty of Azhagar Malai and meditated on Lord Vishnu, asking Him to reside in the beautiful surroundings for the benefit of the people. Responding to Yama’s request, the Lord ordered Viswakarma, the architect of the celestials, to construct a temple for Him there. The Lord took this place as His permanent abode with his consorts, Sri Devi and Bhoo Devi. There is also an interesting story that the water used by Brahma to wash the feet of the Lord in the Trivikrama Avatara passed through the anklets and fell at this kshethram. Hence, the nearby river is called Noopura Gangai or Silambu Aaru. The river water is being used for Tirumanjanam to the deity.

Thotti Tirumanjanam

In the Tamil month of Aipassi, during the Shukla Paksham on the day of Dwadashi, a special utsavam known as Thotti Tirumanjanam is conducted. During this utsavam, the utsava murthy of the Lord is brought outside the temple to a small cave where the Noopura Gangai flows. The Lord’s hair is oiled with medicinal oils, and tirumanjanam is performed with Noopura Gangai falling from a small height on the Lord’s head.
Sri Andal, in one of her Pasurams, had written that she wished to present to Lord Kallazhagar 100 gangalams (a type of vessel made of copper and/or brass), each of butter and pounded rice. It is said that Bhagawad Ramanujar read this pasuram and decided to make her poetic wishes a reality, presenting the Lord with 100 gangalams, each made of butter and pounded rice.

It is said that this Lord was the first among the Tirunangur deities to appear to help Lord Shiva get relief from Brahmahatyadosham. The Lord is said to have given Tirukkoshtiyur Nambigal ( Guru of Srimad Ramanujacharya) the ashta-akshara mantram. Thus, one can find an idol of Tirukkoshtiyur Nambigal here at this kshethram.
Another story recounts how Indra was cursed by Durvasa, a maharishi, which led to the Samudra Manthanam. Once there was a dancer who wanted to impress the goddess, Maha Lakshmi. The dancer performed a very intricate set of dances, and soon the goddess appeared before her, presenting the dancer with a garland. Soon after this, it is said that Sage Durvasa was passing by and saw the lovely garland on the neck of the dancer. The dancer offered the sage the garland and left the scene. It is said that the garland possessed a very fragrant smell that attracted bees. Soon, the sage started to get irritated by the buzzing of the bees and was looking to dispose of the garland when Indra arrived atop his mount, Airavata. Durvasa presented the garland to Indra. Airavata took the garland, but instead of throwing it on Indra, it crushed it beneath its legs. Durvasa was immensely angered by this insult and cursed Indra, saying he and the world would lose all their wealth. As the phrasing of the curse was vague, all wealth-bearing substances and creatures, such as the Kalpa Vriksha, Kamadhenu, and even the Goddess Lakshmi, disappeared. Indra never knew a world without getting whatever he desired.
Thus, to regain his lost wealth, Indra is said to have performed tapas here. The Lord is said to have appeared here and given him the idea to perform Samudra Mathanam.
***Tirumangai Azhwar, in his pasuram, starts to address the Lord as nanda villake ananthakariyay, which translates to an Upanishad-Vaakyam which describes the Lord as सत्यम् ज्ञानम् अनंतम् ब्रह्म. The word-for-word translation of this gives us:
सत्यम् – The One who does not change and is the One true Universal Truth.
ज्ञानम् – The most knowledgeable. One who knows everything. Past, present, and future.
अनंतम् – The One who has no end by any cause.
Tirumangai Azhwar refers to the Lord as Nanda Villake, which means a figurative burning lamp, signifying the Upanishad-Vaakyam.

The deity Satyagirinathan is depicted in a reclining posture inside a rock-cut temple. Garuda, Markandeya, and Brahma flank him, all witnessing the events that unfold around Him. According to tradition, the demons Madhu and Kaitabha stole the Vedas and attempted to abduct Mahalakshmi. She is shown in the panel, frightened and hiding near the Lord’s tiruvadi. In response, Adisesha, who serves as the Lord’s bed, emits poisonous fumes in the form of jwala (fiery orbs) to frighten the demons. The Lord is said to have retrieved the Vedas and protected Mahalakshmi from harm.
The panel shows both Madhu, who is soft by nature, and Kaitabha, who is fierce and aggressive, advancing toward the Lord. On one side, Bhoomadevi approaches the Lord seeking refuge at the Lord’s tiruvadi. Sri Devi is seen near the head of Adisesha, also seeking refuge. The Lord raises His hand to offer assurance to Sri Devi and lifts His gaze toward Bhoomadevi to reassure her.
Above the Lord, Adisesha is seen releasing the jwala from his mouth, directed at the demons. At the top of the composition, Yama Dharmaraja and Chitragupta are depicted recording the moment in their ledger, signifying that the end of Madhu and Kaitabha is near.
The entire episode is captured within a single panel, carved in stone. It includes the fear of Mahalakshmi, the supplication of Bhoomadevi and Sri Devi, the aggression of the demons, the Lord’s protective gestures, the fury of Adisesha, and the presence of Yama and Chitragupta as cosmic witnesses. The depiction is dynamic and composed, presenting a complete narrative within a single visual frame.

Modern-day Nagapattinam was believed to be a dense forest back in the Krita Yugam known as Sundara-Aranyam. The town is said to have derived its name from Nagapattinam, as Nagaraja Adiseshan had performed tapas here in the Lord's honor.
 The Lord here is said to have shown Himself to Dhruva. The story is as follows.
Dhruva was the son of King Uttanapada. Uttanapada had two wives, named Suruchi and Suneethi. Suruchi was a very pompous and cruel person. She had a son named Uttama. Suruchi was hell-bent on outshining Suneethi in anything she did. On one occasion, when Uttanapada was sitting on the throne in the throne room, Dhruva approached Uttanapada and asked him if he could sit on his lap. No sooner had Dhruva asked than Suruchi dragged him away from his father and put Uttama on his father’s lap. She told Dhruva that he was in no way blessed to sit on his father’s lap and further went on to insult Suneethi by telling Dhruva that he wasn’t destined for greatness as he was born in Suneethi’s womb. She told him never to try approaching his father ever again. Dhruva innocently went to his mother and told her what had happened. She told Dhruva that if he couldn’t sit on his father’s lap, it was no big deal, as another father would accept anyone. She told Dhruva that Lord Sriman Narayana would never reject his requests. Hearing his mother’s words, Dhruva went into the forests, committed to performing penance to see the Lord. When Dhruva went into the forest, he was greeted by Narada, who described the Lord’s appearance to Dhruva. Sage Narada instructed Dhruva to visualize a dark-complexioned person with a conch-like neck, broad shoulders, slender hips, coral-like lips, lotus-like feet, and four hands holding the Shanka, Chakra, Gadha, and Padma in each hand.
Given the Lord’s appearance, Dhruva, without any second thought in his head, started his penance to see the Lord. The Lord was soon impressed by seeing a five-year-old boy and appeared before Dhruva. The boy, upon seeing the Lord, was dumbstruck and didn’t know what to say. The Lord then touched the boy’s cheek with the Panchajanyam and brought out the boy’s voice. The innocence and devotion shown by the boy touched the Lord, who granted him and his mother a special position beyond the Brahmandam and told him that it would become known as the Dhruva Mandalam. When the boy could not get any attention from his father, he turned to see the Lord, who granted him far more than he ever asked for.

Legend tells the story of nine yogis who offered worship to the Lord present at this kshethram and attained moksham. According to the rules of prathistapana (the process of establishing the Lord in stone), the Lord is established, and all associated rituals are performed, sealing the Lord in the garbha-griha for eight days. Thus, the first yogi performed prathistapana of the Lord and opened the door of the garbha-griha after eight days. When he opened the doors, he found the Lord missing. Similarly, eight of the nine yogis found the Lord missing from the garbha-griha. The ninth yogi performed the prathistapana of the Lord, but instead of waiting eight days, he opened the door on the third day. The yogi found that the Lord was slowly sinking into the earth in the garbha-griha. The yogi then concluded that the Lords previously established by the other eight yogis must have also sunk into the earth in the same manner. Thus, the yogi asked the Lord to stop sinking into the ground and asked Him to remain there at the kshethram to serve all the devotees who would visit the kshethram. Thus, when one visits this kshethram, they can only see the Lord above the waist.
This is the only temple in the Malainadu Divyadesams that houses Lakshmi Devi separately in a shrine.

*** It is said the Lord here is prathyaksham to Gajendran and Sri Lakshmi. It is said that there was a competition between Gajendran and Lakshmi Devi as to who would present the Lord with a lotus first. One day, Gajendran asked the Lord to allow his devotee to perform kainkaryam (divine service to the Lord). Thus, the Lord requested Lakshmi Devi to come and sit next to Him and enjoy the divine service, and not to engage in any competition with the devotees.

Narakasura was the son of Bhoomi Devi. Having allied himself with Banasura, Naraka became a force to be reckoned with. To show his power, Naraka had kidnapped 16001 maidens and was planning to offer them to Kamakya Devi.  Naraka then attacked Amaravati, the heavenly capital of Indra. Naraka stormed into Amaravati and stole all of Indra’s elephants, Varuna’s Umbrella, and mother Aditi’s earrings. As Naraka was to attack Indra, Indra mounted Airavata and fled to Dwarka to seek the help and protection of Lord Shree Krishna. Indra narrated what had happened at Amaravati and asked Krishna to bring back Mother Aditi’s earrings. Lord Krishna, along with Satyabhama, mounts the Lord’s vehicle, Garuda, and leaves for Pragjyothisham (modern-day Assam), the kingdom of Naraka.
To stop intruders from entering his kingdom, Naraka had set up elaborate traps to take care of any who was daring enough to try and challenge him. Lord Krishna destroyed all the traps that were laid one by one. The first trap was a divine boulder that would crush anyone who tried to enter the border. The Lord destroyed the boulder with his mace. The second trap was a swirling pit of fire that would rise and engulf anyone who passed the first trial. The Lord sent his Sudharshana Chakra into the pit. The Chakra engulfed the flames and absorbed them. The last trap that was laid was a demon named Mura. Mura was the commander-in-chief of Naraka’s army. Mura tried his best to keep the Lord at bay but was easily defeated. Following the death of Mura, his seven sons tried to avenge his death, but all of them were easily defeated. Finally, Naraka showed himself and had a long battle with the Lord. At the end of the battle, Lord Shree Krishna emerged victoriously. Naraka, in his dying breath, asked Krishna for a boon. He asked that one day in a year, to let Ganga reach everyone so that they can atone for the sins that might have been committed by them knowingly or unknowingly. Lord Krishna granted the boon and said that day would henceforth be referred to as Naraka Chaturdashi. After Naraka’s death, the Lord freed all the maidens and is said to have married all of them to protect them. He also placed Naraka’s son Bhagadatta on the throne of Pragjyothisham and recovered Indra’s elephants, Varuna’s umbrella, and mother Aditi’s earrings.
When Lord Shree Krishna and Satyabhama reached Tirukavalampadi, Satyabhama is said to have asked the Lord to bring her the divine Parijatham flower. Thus, the Lord went back to Indra and asked that he spare a flower for the sake of Satyabhama. Indra promptly refused, saying the divine flower does not belong on Bhulokam. Lord Shree Krishna is then said to have defeated Indra and established a Parijatham garden here at this Kshethram.
***The specialty of these eleven temples together is the Padhnor Garudothasavam(eleven Garudothsavam) that takes place together during Thai Maasam(January 15- February 15) on the day of Amavasya.

The legend tells the story of Tirumangai Azhwar visiting this kshethram. When he visited this kshethram, the hill was surrounded by water, hence giving the kshethram the name Tiruneermalai. This kshethram features shrines for Ranganatha Perumal, Ulagalantha Perumal, and Shantha Nrisimha Perumal atop a small hillock. At the base of the hillock, one can find the temple of Neervana Perumal and a shrine for Rama, Lakshmana, Bharatha, Shatrughna, along with Devi Sita.
It is said that Maharishi Valmiki visited this kshethram and paid his homage to the Lords atop the hill, but was not satisfied by his darshan of the Lords. Thus, he requested the Lords to show themselves as Lord Rama. Therefore, the Lords collectively took the form of Rama. Sridevi and Bhudevi became Devi Sita. Adisesha, Shankam, and Chakra appeared as Lakshmana, Bharatha, and Shatrugna, and Garuda as Hanuman.
*** As one enters the premises of the Neervana Perumal temple, they can see that the Dwaja-Sthambam is displaced and not in line with the entrance, and the same is true with the position of the garbha griha of Neervana Perumal. This is because when Lord Rama appeared, he assumed the primary deity of the kshethram, displacing the position of Neervana Perumal. The Dwaja-Sthambam is in line with Sri Ramar.

Shree Krishna told the Pandavas that he would, for the last time, visit the court of Hastinapur and try his hand at imploring reason to Duryodhana, trying to make him realize that nothing good could come out of a war. Shree Krishna arrived in Hastinapur and, instead of staying in the palace, chose to spend some time with Vidura. He stayed the night at Vidura’s house and in the morning went to the court of Hastinapur to try and convince Duryodhana out of the idea of war. Krishna presented his argument, asking that if the Kauravas did not want to return the entire kingdom, then at least provide the Pandavas with five villages.
Duryodhana, in a crimson fury, snapped at Krishna, saying that he was not qualified to come to the court with such an issue and told him to go back to herding cattle. He further told Krishna that he would not give even a single needle-head’s worth of land. He then instructed the guards to tie Krishna up and make him a prisoner. As the guards were tying Krishna, he started to grow to an immeasurable height and took his Vishwaroopam Form. 
Vaisampayana Maharishi was narrating the Bhagavatham to Janamejaya and was referring to Lord Krishna’s visit to Hastinapuram as the Pandavas' Dhoota (Ambassador). Desiring to have the Vishwaroopa darsana, they performed Ashwamedhayagam at Kanchipuram. On completion of the yagam, the Lord gave darshan as Pandavadhootar. There are shrines for Ramanuja Acharya and Manavaala Maamunigal.

This kshethram is the ultimate destination for any jeevaatma. This kshethram lies beyond Tiruparkadal. Sri Vaikuntham is described as a mesmerizing place from which there is no return, as specified in the Vedas and Upanishads as  “na cha punara avarthathe na cha punara avarthathe na cha punara avarthathe.” The Lord is seen as Sri Paramapadanathan, sitting alongside Him atop Adiseshan are Sridevi, Bhudevi, and Neeladevi. After the jeevaathma crosses Ksheerabdi, it will be guided to the borders of Sri Vaikuntham. Here flows the Viraja River. The jeevaathma is allowed to bathe in the Viraja River, where the divine river washes away any residual sins. Upon entering Sri Vaikuntham, the jeevaathma will see all the gods singing the praise of the Lord, which is described as “tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṁ padaṁ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ.” After being mesmerized by all of this, the jeevaathma will go and finally see the Lord Himself. The Lord gives space on his lap and asks the jeevaathma what took it so long to reach Him. The jeevaathma has no response but to say it has finally attained Him. The jeevaathma then offers itself to become one with the Lord. It asks the Lord to give it space inside His Heart to attain moksham. The jeevaathma asks the Lord to imagine it to be a single grain of rice, and that grain is being offered solely and wholeheartedly to Him. The Lord then places the jeevaathma near His heart, merging the jeevaathma with Himself, the Paramaathma, granting moksham. The Lord present here is said to be a vyuha-roopam of Paravasudevan who resides in Sri Vaikuntham. Empurumaan presents Himself as Vasudevan, Sankarshanan, Pradyumnan, and Anirudhan, who are said to be vyuha-roopam of the Lord. Vasudevan is the creator, Sankarshanan is the sustainer, Pradyumnan is the destroyer, and Anirudhan represents divine knowledge. These vyuha-roopam are further said to divide into three forms each. Vasudevan is said to represent equivalence to Keshava, Madhava, and Narayana. Sankarshanan is said to represent equivalence to Govinda, Vishnu, and Madhusoodhan. Pradyumana is said to represent equivalence to Trivikrama, Vamana, and Sridhara. Anirudhan is said to represent the equivalence to Rishikesha, Padmanabhan, and Damodara.
The twelve of these forms are referred to as the 12 Sooriyars and Chandirans, who are found in all 12 directions. They are responsible for bringing all Jeevaathmas into existence, guiding their lives, and calculating their Paavam and Punyam.
The Ashtaakshara mantram is said to always resonate in this kshethram. To reach this kshethram, one must learn the ashtaakshara mantram from a guru and meditate upon Sri Ksheerabdi Nathan.

Once King Upamanyu (Pandya King) had gone hunting in the forest to hunt a rogue elephant, he accidentally killed a brahmin who was performing tapas by the banks of a river. In repentance for his act, the king renounced his throne and began roaming the vast expanse of his former kingdom. When the king reached Tiruperrnagar, Lord Shiva appeared in front of the king and told him to serve food to a  thousand brahmins daily with appam. The king started to follow the instructions that he had received. One day, Lord Vishnu decided to participate in the king’s daily meal service. The Lord came in the disguise of a brahmin and approached the king, saying He was very hungry and asked that He be fed. The king asked the brahmin to wait until he had fed the remaining brahmins who had assembled before Him. The Lord was very strong with His claim and demanded that He be fed first. The king obliged and served the brahmin food.
To the king’s astonishment, the brahmin ate all the food that was prepared for the gathered thousand brahmins. The king then asked the brahmin if he was satisfied with the meal. The Brahmin said he was still hungry and asked the king to give him an appam, as it had not been served to him. No sooner had the king obtained a pitcher (kudam) with the appam than the Brahmin snatched the kudam from the king’s hands. Immediately, the Lord turned into an idol reclining on Adiseshan, putting his hand inside the kudam. Hence, the Lord gained the name Appa Kuduthan. At the same time, Markandeya Maharishi was directed by Lord Shiva to pray to Lord Vishnu for the gift of longevity. When Markandeya Maharishi reached the kshethram, the Lord removed his hand from the kudam and blessed him with the longevity of life and also relieved the king of his Brahmahatidosham.
Another story tells the tale of Kamalavalli Thayaar asking the Lord to get her Parijaatham flowers. Parijaatham flowers are divine flowers that grow in the gardens of Indra. When the Lord approached Indra to obtain some flowers for Thayaar, Indra refused to acknowledge that the Paarijatham was a divine flower and did not belong in Bhoolokam. He further tried to hurl the Vajraayudham on the Lord when the Lord was persistent with His request. The Lord, in his shayanam, raised his left hand and plucked the Vajraayudham from Indra’s hand. Indra then provided the flowers, consisting of defeat at the Lord’s hands. Thus, the vimanam and pushkarani here are named in Indra’s honor as he provided the Parijaatham.

The legend states that this temple was established by Arjuna during his trip to South India, when he was in vanavaasam with the Pandavas. It is said that when Arjuna reached this kshethram, he was extremely thirsty and went in search of water. When he could find no water, he found Agastya Maharishi performing tapas. Arjuna paid his respects to the Maharishi and asked him if he had any water. Agastya Maharishi said all the water he could offer was that which was there in his kamandalam. After Arjuna drank the water, he asked the sage if he could direct him to a source of water, as he was still thirsty. Agastya Maharishi said there was no water in the area and told Arjuna to seek the help of Lord Krishna, as he always did. Arjuna then performs tapas to call Lord Krishna to this kshethram. When Lord Krishna arrived, he gave Arjuna a sword and asked Arjuna to dig the earth. When Arjuna dug the earth, a stream of water emerged, granting water to the area. This water source came to be known as Kadga Theertham( the water that came from the sword).


***Here, one can see Lord Parthasarathy with four hands, as supposed to see him with two hands like at Tiruvallikeni(Chennai). Another specialty of this kshethram is that one can see the utsava moorthigal of both Lord Rama and Lord Krishna standing in the same garbha-graham. We can see Kolavili Ramar holding the shankam, chakram, bow, and arrow.

According to legend, Durvasa Maharishi is said to have once visited Karya-Vaikuntham, but Bhoodevi ignored his arrival and did not perform the required athithi-sathkaaram. Thus, Durvasa Maharishi is said to have cursed Bhoodevi, stating that she would become like Sridevi. When the Lord takes His avatars, He stands, sits, lies down, and performs all His activities on Bhoodevi, whereas He has allocated a small position in His heart for Sridevi. Upon hearing this curse, Bhoodevi pleads with the Maharishi to forgive her. Durvasa Maharishi tells Bhoodevi that once a curse is delivered, it cannot be taken back, but she could attain atonement if she performed tapas at Tirupperai. Thus, Bhoodevi is said to come to this kshethram and perform tapas by chanting the ashtakshara mantram. One day, when Bhoodevi went to bathe in the Tamaraparani River before offering her daily penance, She is said to have found a pair of kundalam (earrings) in the shape of makaram (a type of fish). She is said to have presented this makara-kundalam to the Lord, thus relieving Herself from the curse and giving Him the name Makara Nedunkuzhaikkadan.

*** The importance of this kshethram lies in the practice of Varuna Japam. It is said that if one performs Varuna Japam at this kshethram, it will bring rain as desired. It is noted that Varuna sought the help of Makara Nedunkuzhaikkadan Perumal in his time of need.

The legend tells the story of a brahmin named Yagna Sarma. It is said that one evening, when Yagna Sarma and his wife were in a jovial state, Shakthi Maharishi(son of Vasishta Maharishi) is said to have visited their hermitage. Yagna Sarma and his wife failed to recognize that the sage had come to their doorstep and did not perform any kind of athithi-sathkaaram(service to the guest). Shakthi Maharishi, in a fit of rage, cursed Yagna Sarma that he would become a demon. Yagna Sarma begged for the sage’s forgiveness and asked him if there was any way out of this curse. The sage then tells Yagna Sarma that Indra would perform a yagnam at Tiruppulingudi, and he is to go and try to disrupt this yagnam. When this would happen, Indra would hurl his vajra-aayudam, releasing him from the effects of the curse. As the sage predicted, Yagna Sarma went in his demonic form to disrupt the yagnam, and Indra hurled his vajra-aayudam at the demon, killing Yagna Sarma. Indra was performing a prayashchita-yagnam as he had unknowingly killed a sage who was performing tapas in the form of a deer. When the yagnam reached its completion, the Lord is said to have appeared, granting atonement to Indra and moksham to Yagna Sarma.
Another story tells that there was a feud between Bhudevi and Sridevi. Bhudevi claimed that the Lord spends too much time with Sridevi and does not spend enough time with Her. The Lord is said to have solved the problem by placing Bhudevi on one side of His tiruvadigal(His lotus feet) and Sridevi on the other, and constantly looking at both of them, showing that in His eyes, both of them are equal. Thus, when one stands outside the garbha-griha, they cannot see the Lord’s tiruvadigal. To see the Lord’s tiruvadigal, there is a small window on the outside of the garbha-griha through which we can see His tiruvadigal while performing pradakshinam.

Legend has it that Adi Jagannatha Perumal is said to have been present at this kshetram even before Dasharatha came with Kaikeyi to conquer South India. It is noted that Dasharatha performed tapas to this Lord to have children.
Legend tells that Lord Rama reached the seashore where Vibhishana performed sharanagathi. As the army contemplated how to cross the ocean, Vibhishana advised Lord Rama to pray to Samudraraja by performing praayopavesham (fast for three days and nights) to allow their passage over his waters to reach Lanka. Thus, Lord Rama is said to have sat in Padmasanam on a bed made of darbha grass with the Anjali mudra for three days. When Samudraraja did not show himself, in a rage, Lord Rama told Lakshmana to hand Him His bow and an arrow. The Lord mounts the arrow and tells Samudraraja that He would make all the water in the ocean evaporate if he did not show himself. As the Lord was about to fire His deadly weapon, Samudraraja appears and falls at Lord Rama’s feet and tells the army that Nal and Neel were phenomenal architects and that they could build a bridge that would float on the oceanic waters, granting Lord Rama and His army passage over the ocean to Sri Lanka. As Lord Rama sat on a bed made of darbha, this kshethram is called Pullaranya Kshethram.
*** The water at this kshethram is considered very holy, as it was the starting point of the Ramasethu. Thus, taking a bath here or sethu-snanam is considered to absolve all sins. Along with sethu-snanam, performing tarpanam here at this kshetram is considered highly auspicious.

During the Ramayana period, when Ravana abducted Devi Sita and started to fly away in the Pushpaka Vimanam, a vulture by the name of Jatayu stood in his way and put up a valiant battle against Ravana until Ravana cut off Jatayu’s wings, causing him to fall in the Panchavati forest. Jatayu held on to his life till he could see Lord Rama and tell him what had transpired so far. After relaying the information of Devi Sita’s kidnapping to Lord Rama, Jatayu lost his life. Lord Rama is then supposed to have cremated Jatayu, offering him salvation(moksham). The Lord here is holding Jatayu on His lap to cremate him.

***A peculiarity of this kshethram is that Sridevi Thayaar and Bhudevi Thayaar have interchanged places, i.e., Bhudevi Thayaar is on the right, and Sridevi Thayaar is on the left. When one sees Sridevi Thayaar here, one can observe that she is standing about two feet behind the Lord, as She was unable to handle the heat of the pyre. 
On new moon day (Amavasya), pilgrims congregate here at this kshethram to perform tharpanam(rites to the departed souls). In this temple, barren women receive the prasadam, which consists of roasted lentils soaked in water. While taken home, it is believed that if the lentils sprout, they will beget children.

It is said that Lord Rama was responsible for establishing this temple at this kshethram. After defeating Ravana, Lord Rama was faced with Brahmanhatyadosham, as he had killed Ravana, who was born a Brahmin. To engage in pariharam for the dosha, the Lord was seeking solutions. It was then that Dridanetramuni suggested to the Lord that he make an idol of a cow out of pure gold, large enough for the Lord to remain seated within it. Dridanetramuni then asked the Lord to remain seated within the gold edifice for four days, following which he requested that the Lord engage in charitable activities. The Lord did as he was instructed. After the four days had passed, Lord Rama donated the gold idol to Dridanetramuni. When Dridanetramuni returned to his ashram near Sirkazhi, he sold the gold statue to raise money for the temple's construction. Hence, the temple is called Semponsei (Sempon-gold, Sei-made of) Kovil.
*** Lord Rama is said to have performed daily rituals for the Lord here.

Swami Vedanta Desikan:
Swami Desikan is considered to be an incarnation of the divine bell of Sri Venkateshwara Swami of Tirumalai. Swami Desikan was born here in Tooppul to Sri Anantha Suri and Devi Totaramba. By birth, Swami Desikan was named Venkatanatha. When Swami Desikan was just five years of age, he was taken by his maternal uncle, Kidambi Appular, to attend a discourse by Nadadhoor Ammal, a revered Sri Vaishnava Scholar at the time. As soon as Nadadhoor Ammal saw Venkatanatha, he saw a divine radiance in the child and stopped his lecture to hug the child affectionately. After this, when Nadadhoor Ammal said that he had forgotten where he had stopped his lecture, Venkatanatha reminded him of where he had stopped. This act astonished the crowd, as they had never seen a five-year-old boy comprehend the deep intricacies of philosophical knowledge being discussed. It was then that Nadadhoor Ammal predicted and blessed Venkatanatha, stating that he would become the torch-bearer to spread Sri Vaishnavism everywhere in the future.
At each place, he composed numerous works in languages such as Tamil, Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Manipravalam (a blend of Sanskrit and Tamil), which revealed his ingenuity, creativity, logic, linguistic expertise, devotional fervor, and erudite scholarship.

The Lord here is standing along with His four consorts, namely, Sridevi, Bhoodevi, Neeladevi, and Jambhavathi.
Jambhavathi is the daughter of Jambavan, who is seen in the Ramayana. The story of how the Lord married Jambhavathi is as follows. Lord Krishna’s royal treasurer Satrajit, used to house the Syamantaka Mani ( a divine gem that is said to give an unlimited amount of treasure ). Once, Lord Krishna is said to have asked to see this gem, but Satrajit refused. Soon, one day, Satrajit’s brother is said to have worn the gem and gone out into the forest to hunt and did not return. When Satrajit noticed that the gem was missing, he blamed it on Krishna, saying He had stolen it. Lord Krishna is said to have gone into the forest to prove his innocence. When the Lord was deep in the forest, He found Satrajit’s brother’s body covered in the mauling of a lion. He decided to check around the area further and soon saw a glimmering twinkle emanating from a nearby cave. When He went to probe the source of the twinkle, He noticed the gem in the hands of a female bear and approached her to claim the gem and clear His name when another male bear attacked Him. Lord Krishna fought a long-drawn battle with the bear, with neither side giving in. Soon, Lord Krishna realized that the bear was none other than Jambavan, one of His generals in the time of the Ramayana. Lord Krishna reveals Himself as Lord Rama to Jambavan, and their fight comes to an end. Jambavan returns the gem to Lord Krishna, and along with the gem, he gives his daughter’s hand in marriage to Lord Krishna. The female bear is transformed into a beautiful maiden, who is Jambhavathi.
This kshethram is where Aniruddha was married to Banasura’s daughter, Usha. The story is as follows.
Banasura was the king of Sonitpur (a modern-day district in Assam). Bana was an ardent devotee of Lord Shiva. By the grace of Lord Shiva, Bana had received a thousand hands with which he used to play the mridangam for the Lord. One day, when Lord Shiva was dancing, he granted Banasura a boon that he would personally protect him no matter the circumstance. Banasura had a daughter named Usha. Usha was an ardent devotee of Devi Parvati.  Devi Parvati blesses Usha, saying a man would appear in her dream,s and he would be the one that she would get married to. After a few days, Usha had a dream of a man. He had broad shoulders, a slender waist, coral-like lips, a lotus-like face, and eyes that seemed to resemble the sun and the moon. Usha had a friend named Chitralekha who could draw an exact copy of any description that was placed before her. Thus, as Usha described, Chitralekha drew a picture of the man she dreamed of. When both of them went through to see who the person in the photo was, they discovered that the person in the picture was Aniruddha, the grandson of Shree Krishna. Chitralekha also possessed another power, enabling her to teleport herself to any place she wished and bring back anyone she willed. Therefore, at night, Usha asked Chitralekha to bring Aniruddha to the palace without her father realizing, as her father was a sworn enemy of Shree Krishna.
Chitralekha did as instructed and brought Aniruddha to Usha’s royal quarters. Soon, news reached Banasura, saying Usha was enjoying the company of an unknown man within her personal quarters. Banasura rushed in a fury and bound Aniruddha with a thousand snakes. The news was then sent to Dwarka that Banasura was holding both Usha and Aniruddha hostage. Krishna, along with Balarama, immediately left for Sonitpur on Garuda. As soon as Krishna and Balarama reached Sonitpur, they challenged Banasura to war and demanded that Aniruddha be released and that Usha be married to Aniruddha. Banasura refused and commanded his army to attack Krishna and Balarama. Krishna and Balarama effortlessly beat Banasura’s army.
Soon, Banasura was left alone to face Krishna and Balarama, having prayed to Lord Shiva for protection. Lord Shiva first sent his Ganas to face Krishna and Balarama. When the Ganas were defeated, Lord Shiva himself appeared to face Lord Krishna and Balarama. Lord Shiva and Lord Krishna engaged in a fierce battle, neither side yielding an inch. Lord Shiva was soon left with only his set of divyastras. Lord Shiva released the Pashupatastra, and in response, Lord Krishna released the Narayana-Astra. The divine weapons clashed, creating massive explosions. Finally, Lord Shiva executed his final weapon in the form of a plague called Rudra-Jwaram. Lord Krishna replied to this in the form of an antidote called Vaishnava-Jwaram. Lord Krishna countered Lord Shiva completely, while Lord Balarama defeated Lord Karthikeya. Banasura was now bereft of any protection and open to attack. Lord Krishna then sent his Sudharshana Chakra behind Banasura. Sudharshana chased after Banasura and cut off 996 of his 1000 arms. Banasura was left completely humiliated, and he had no other choice but to comply with the wishes of Lord Krishna and Balarama. Aniruddha and Usha were released from prison and got married.

According to Srimad Bhagavatham, Lord Vishnu, in His incarnations as Nara and Narayana, performed deep tapas for time immemorial for the well-being of all living entities. According to legend, when Nara and Narayana were performing tapas in a place where Badri trees were growing. At one point, the sunlight became very intense. Thus, to protect the Lord from the sunlight, Lakshmi Devi is said to have taken the form of a Badri tree and grown in such a way as to provide shade to the Lord.
This fact is reiterated in the Mahabharata when Lord Krishna tells Arjuna that in their previous lives, Arjuna was the manifestation of Nara, and He was the manifestation of Narayana. The Pandavas are said to have visited this kshethram before embarking on their final journeys to Mana, from where they left their bodies to reach Paramapadam. Mana is 4 km from this kshethram.
This is one of the Swayam-Vyaktha Kshethrams. It is said that there are five Badri kshethrams. Together, they are known as Pancha Badri Kshethram. Vishal Badri (Badrinath Temple installed by Sri Adi Shankaracharya), Yogadhyan Badri (where the Lord is in a meditative posture), Bhavishya Badri (Badri of the future), Vridha Badri (the original shrine where Vishwakarma carved the idol), Adi Badri. It is said that the Lord appeared in Sri Adi Shankaracharya’s dream and told him that he would find His idol inside the tapta-kundam ( hot springs ) present outside, where the present-day temple is situated. It is said that Sri Adi Shankaracharya dipped in the spring multiple times before finding the Lord’s idol. To date, the pooja is performed by nambudhri brahmins who follow the Kerala style of pooja.

Badrinath Temple: Raval Ji opening and entering the temple in the early morning.

The only time one can see the true form of the Lord is during the Tirumanjanam/abhishekham, which takes place around 5 am.

*** The utsava murthy, i.e., Parthasarathy Perumal, can be seen with scars that are said to have been inflicted on Him by Bheeshma during the Mahabharata war.

History:
According to legend, there was once a Nambudhri Priest by the name of Bilwa Mangala Samiyar who used to perform Tiruvaradhanam daily to many Shalagramams. It is said that there was a young boy who accompanied the priest daily during his kanikaryams. The boy was very naughty, but had told the priest not to question anything that he would do. One day, the boy stole some of the Shalagramams from the priest and started to run. The priest pursued the boy. As the chase continued, the boy ran into a dense forest known as Ananthavanam. As the priest ran after the boy, a humungous illupa-maram (Indian Butter Tree) fell in front of him. The height of the tree can be comprehended as follows. It is said that the Lord’s tirumukham rested in Tiruvattar, His nabhi rested in Thiruvananthapuram, and his tiruvadi rested in a place known as Tirupaapur.
Similarly, another story states that Diwakara Maharishi chased a boy into the Ananthavanam, and the tree fell; as a result, the Lord appeared in the tree. It is said that Diwakara Maharishi was holding a tridandam, and he asked the Lord to reduce his length to match the tridandam. Thus, the Lord shrank Himself to a length of 18 feet. As the Lord shrank Himself from a humungous length to a more viewable length, He got the name Ananthapadhmanabhan. Anantha, which means immeasurable, and Padmanabhan, as Lord Brahma emanates from the divine lotus in His navel. Thus, a temple was constructed, and the Lord was present in a wooden form for many years. Even today, one can get a sight of Bilwa Mangala Samiyar as well as Diwakara Maharishi inside the garbha-griha.

Modern Day:
In 1686, a massive fire reportedly broke out in the temple. The then king Marthanda Varman is said to have reconstructed the temple over the course of forty years and performed the samprokshanam for the temple in 1726. It is said that the Lord appeared in the king’s dream and told him that He wished to be converted into a shila-vigraham form. It is said that elephants carried 2400 shalagramams on their heads from Nepal and delivered them to the king. The Lord further instructed the king to use 1200 shalagramams to constitute Him in the shila-vigraham form. The remaining shalagramams were to be stored safely till they would be necessary to reconstruct the Lord once more. To this day, that requirement has not arisen. In the year 1750, Marthanda Varman is said to have written down all his wealth in the name of the Lord and the temple and given his family the title of Padmanabha-Dasan, which translates to those who serve Lord Padmanabha. To this day, the Kings of the Travancore family visit the temple in the early hours of the morning and pay their respects to the Lord. Due to being unable to visit the temple on any given day, they pay a fine to the temple. There are two annual festivals during the Tamil months of Panguni and Aippasi.

The significance of the three doors for viewing the Lord:
Given the length of the Lord being eighteen feet, there are three doors through which one can view the Lord. In the first door, one can see the Lord’s tirumukham. This door is said to have been meant for the Nityasooris, such as Garudan and Vishwaksenar. In the second door, one can see the Lord’s naabhi (navel) from which emanates the divine lotus, inside which is seated Lord Brahma. This door is said to have been meant for the Devas. In the third door, one can see the Lord’s tiruvadi (His holy lotus-feet). This door is said to be meant for all His devotees who seek his refuge as instructed by Him in the Gita, where Lord Krishna says, “Sarva Dharman Parityajya maam ekam sharanam vraja.”

*** Other specialties in this temple include Anjaneya Swami, who is always adorned in butter. There is a shrine hosting Ugra-Narasimha Swami. To keep the Lord’s anger under control, Valmiki Ramayana Parayanam is done daily in front of the shrine.

The legend tells the tale of the Lord defeating the demon named Adikeshi. After his death, Adikeshi's wife performs penance and asks the Ganga and Tamraparani rivers to flow in a circular pattern, engulfing the area. The Lord is said to have taken His reclining form and slept atop the demon, using Adisesha as His bed, at the meeting point of the rivers. Seeing that her efforts to take revenge were in vain, Adikeshi's wife is said to have surrendered to the Lord.
Another story tells us how the Lord came to take His current form. There was a Maharishi named Hathalekar, who was very short in stature but extremely learned from a young age. One day, the Lord decided to test Hathalekar Maharishi. He approached and began teasing the sage about his height. At one point, when the sage was standing next to a banana tree, the Lord asked if his parents were dwarves too, having given birth to someone of his stature. The sage, in a fit of anger, pointed at the tree and said, “These are my parents.”
Not wanting to disappoint His devotee, the Lord caused the parents to emerge from the tree, and then gave him upadesham of the Ashtaakshara mantram, telling the sage that it had all been a test of his faith and devotion. The Lord, pleased with the sage, then instructed him to reconstruct His form as Adikesava Perumal.
Hathalekar used to perform aaradhanam daily to 16,008 shalagramams. It is said that the Lord was brought into His present form using these 16,008 shalagramams, along with a mixture of karungal (black teak wood) ash, mustard seeds, and jaggery.
As a result, there is no abhishekam performed for the murti at this kshetram. The Lord is preserved through the application of medicinal herbs and oils, as prescribed by the Ayurveda Shastram.
The Lord here is very similar to Sri Ananthapadmanabha Swamy at Thiruvananthapuram. The Adikesava Perumal murti is 22 feet long, compared to 18 feet at Thiruvananthapuram. Another difference lies in the Nabhi Kamalam (navel lotus) of Adikesava Perumal; Lord Brahma is not present, as this form of the Lord is said to have appeared before Brahma was created.
There are three doors through which devotees can have darshan—one to see the Lord's face, one for His navel, and another for His feet.
It is said that Sri Ananthapadmanabha Swamy reclines in such a direction that He faces Adikesava Perumal.

Legend has it that Lord Brahma caused the herds of cattle being grazed by Lord Krishna to disappear, upon which Lord Krishna created another herd. Finding this, Brahma apologized to Krishna and requested Him to take abode at Tiruvazhandur. In the sanctum, Prahlada is to the right of the moolavar and Garudan to His left. After witnessing Narasimha Avataram of the Lord, Prahlada asks to see the lord in a Shantha-Swaroopam (calm form), to which the Lord gave him darshanam at this kshethram. It is said that the vimanam of this kshethram was given by Garudan, hence the name Garuda Vimanam.

*** This kshethram is also the birthplace of the great Tamizh poet Kambar, who has given us the magnum opus of Kamba Ramayanam, which rivals and trumps Valmiki Ramayanam in terms of poetic beauty. One can find a shrine dedicated to Kambar and his wife here at this kshethram.

According to legend, when all of Saraswati Devi’s efforts to stop Lord Brahma’s Ashwamedha Yagnam failed, she decided to flow like a river(a personification of the speed at which she could deliver any knowledge). Thus, she took the form of Vegavathy and decided to flow over the homa kundam. At this point, Lord Brahma requested the Lord to stop Devi Saraswati. Thus, the Lord took this form and acted as a dam, redirecting the flow of the river. Therefore, this kshethram came to be known as Vegavathy Annai, which later became Vegka.
When Thirumizhisai Azhwar was living in Kanchipuram, an old lady who worked as a servant (Daasi) used to clean his house every day. She did this small act of service with full dedication. Pleased by her sincere effort, the Azhwar blessed her and transformed her into a young and beautiful woman.
Soon, her beauty caught the attention of the king of the region. Surprised by her charm, the king married her, and she became the queen. After some time, the king came to know the story behind the transformation and was curious to meet Thirumizhisai Azhwar himself.
Now, Kani Kannan—who was the Azhwar’s close disciple and companion—was called to the palace. The king asked him to request Azhwar to visit the palace and compose a poem in his praise. But Kani Kannan respectfully told the king that Thirumizhisai Azhwar only sings for the Lord Srivaikuntanathan (Sriman Narayana) and that it was not possible for him to write or sing anything to praise a human being.
Still hoping, the king offered Kani Kannan gold, silver, diamonds, and all kinds of riches if he himself would sing in the king’s praise. But Kani Kannan firmly refused, saying he would not sing about any human, no matter the reward. This made the king angry. In his fury, he ordered Kani Kannan to leave Kanchipuram immediately.
Kani Kannan returned to Thirumizhisai Azhwar and explained everything that had happened. Hearing this, the Azhwar decided that if his devotee was being thrown out of the city, he too would leave along with him.
Before leaving, Thirumizhisai Azhwar composed a verse addressing the Lord Yathothakari Perumal (the presiding deity of the Thiruvekka temple). In it, he told the Lord that since Kani Kannan was leaving the city, and he himself was also leaving, Perumal too should get up from his serpent-bed (Adiseshan), roll it up, and leave Kanchipuram.
To everyone’s shock, the Lord actually obeyed. He rose from His resting posture, folded up His bed, and left the temple to follow His devotee.
The king and the people of Kanchipuram were shaken by this miracle. They ran after them, pleaded for forgiveness, and begged Kani Kannan and Azhwar to return. Moved by their repentance, Kani Kannan agreed to come back.
When they returned, Thirumizhisai Azhwar once again sang to the Lord, asking Him to return to the temple and rest on Adiseshan as before. The Lord came back to the Thiruvekka temple and resumed His reclining posture.
Because the Lord acted exactly according to what the Azhwar said—first leaving, then returning—He came to be known as “Sonna Vannam Seitha Perumal”, which means "The Lord who did exactly as He was told."

*** A peculiarity of this kshethram is that when one sees the Lord reclining here, they can notice that the Lord is laterally inverted, i.e., the Lord’s tiruvadi( His lotus feet) are where His head usually rests and vice versa. This is because when Tirumazhisai Azhwar asked the Lord to return, he did not specify in which direction He must rest.

fields.existingValue: It is said that Shibi Chakravarthy, the grandson of Yayati, a ruler of Ayodhya belonging to the Chandravamsham dynasty, once undertook a trip to South India. One night, he decided to stay at the place known as Shwetagiri, which in Sanskrit translates to a hill with white rocks. Shwetagiri in Tamizh may be split as Vella+Arai, which means white hill. One night during his stay, Shibi Chakravarthy’s army chieftain complained that a wild white boar was running around and causing trouble to the army. Hearing this, the king ordered its capture. A few days passed, and the army chieftain came back with a complaint, saying the boar would magically disappear as they got close to catching it. Hearing this, Shibi Chakravarthy himself decided to go after the boar. He took his bow and set out in search of the animal. As he was searching, he saw the boar and began pursuing it. As he chased after the boar in the forest, he saw Sage Markandeya in penance. Seeing the sage, Shibi Chakravarthy offered his respects and went to inquire of the great sage if he had seen a wild boar pass by. The sage immediately directed the king to an anthill near the tree where he was meditating. He tells the king that he was in penance, waiting for the day the king would arrive seeking out a boar. He hands the king a pitcher of milk and asks him to pour the milk down the anthill. The king follows the sage’s instructions and does as he says. As the king poured the milk down the anthill, it began to melt, revealing a beautiful idol of Lord Pundarikakshan. The king wasted no time in installing the idol of the Lord into a temple. Sage Markandeya then tells the king that he should bring three thousand seven hundred Vaishnavas from his kingdom and help them to settle down here. The king immediately returned to Ayodhya and, according to the sage’s instructions, found three thousand seven hundred Vaishnavas and brought them to the temple. As Shibi counted the number of Vaishnavas that he had brought, he discovered that one of them had mysteriously vanished. The Lord then appeared in the king’s dream, saying He was one among the three thousand seven hundred, and told the king that he wanted to experience firsthand what bhakti felt like. In the Garbhagriha, we can see the Lord holding a prayoga chakram, along with His consorts, Sridevi and Bhoodevi, as well as Sooryan, Chandhran, Garudan, and Aadiseshan.

This kshethram is associated with the story of Vamana Avataram. Let us now see the story. It is said that the Lord took this form to defeat the demon king Bali. Bali was a mighty demon king. He was the grandson of Prahalada. Bali was such a powerful demon that he was individually capable of keeping all the Devas at bay. The Devas then approached Lord Vishnu to aid in defeating Bali. Bali was a Chiranjeevi, hence he could not be killed. He could merely be pushed down to Patala-Lokam. The Lord assured the Devas that he would look into the situation. At the same time, Aditi, the mother of the Devas, wanted to make sure that the Lord would be born to her. To ensure this, Aditi used the means of payovratam (a complete milk-based diet over twelve days). The Lord was born in Aditi’s womb to Aditi and Sage Kashyapa. The Lord was born as a dwarf. As soon as he was born, the Lord revealed to Aditi the various stages of his life, and he grew into a young boy. The upanayanam ceremony was performed, and each of the gods presented Vamana with a gift. Brahma gave him a kamandalam, and Brihaspati gave him the umbrella. Thus, the Lord set out to fulfill the promise given to the Devas. He reached Bali’s palace, where he was giving alms to the brahmins assembled. As the Lord reached the assembly, Shukracharya warned Bali that the person responsible for killing his grandfather had come to defeat him. He advised Bali not to give alms to him. Bali was honored that the Lord had come to his assembly. He proceeded with the program and soon reached Vamana. Bali asked him what he desired as alms. The boy replies, saying all he desires is three paces of land. Bali granted the boy’s wish. To prevent Bali from giving alms, Shukracharya assumed a tiny form and sat at the mouth of Bali’s kamandalam. When water did not come out of the kamandalam, Lord Vamana took a dharba grass and poked the opening of the kamandalam. In the process of poking the opening, Lord Vamana poked one of Shukracharya’s eyes. In pain, Shukracharya left the opening of the kamandalam. The boy started to grow. With the first step, he measured the entire earth. With the second step, he took the heavens. By the time he had to take the third step, there was no space left. Bali got onto his knees and, with a posture of namaskaram, bent his head and asked the Lord to place the third step on his head and push him into Patala-Lokam. The Lord, now in his Trivikrama form, fulfills Bali’s wish and places the third step on his head, sending him to Patala-Lokam. 
It is said that Shukracharya performed tapas here, and the Lord appeared as Kolavilli Ramar, reclined in the bhujanga shayanam, and granted Shukracharya his eye once again.  

***This is one of the special kshethrams in which one can find Lord Rama in a reclining posture.

This kshethram derives its name from the root words "Vel," meaning "desire," and "Irukkai," meaning "place of stay." Thus, the kshethram became Velukkai. It is said that the Lord came here out of his desire to meditate after killing Hiranyakashipu. He also killed all the demons that infested the surrounding land.
Devi Saraswati, in her first attempt to send demons, was unsuccessful, as Lord Ashtabhujar defeated all of them. In her second attempt to spoil the yagnam by creating darkness, she was again unsuccessful, as Lord Deepaprakasar provided a source of light. In a third attempt to stop the yagnam from taking place, She created a mighty demon named Kapalika and unleashed him upon the land. The Lord is then supposed to have taken the form of Nrisimha and killed the demon, therefore protecting the yagnam.
It is said that the Lord presiding over this kshethram was initially Lord Vishnu, facing east. However, when Brighu Maharishi asked to see him in the form of Nrisimha, he took the form of Azhagiyasinga Perumal.

“Vina Venkatesham na natho na natha, Sada venkatesham smarami, smarami,
Hare Venkatesha, praseedha praseedha, Priyam Venkatesha, prayacha prayacha.”
The meaning of the above shlokam is as follows:
“Without you, Oh Venkateshwara, I would not exist. I keep remembering your name. Please bestow me with your love and grace.”
“Venkatadri Samam Sthaanam Brahmande Naasti Kinchanaa…
Venkatesha Samo Devo Na Bhootho Na Bhavishyati..”
The meaning of the above shlokam is as follows:
“Neither in the past nor the future would there be a sacred place in this universe that can equal the sanctity of the Venkatadri hills, nor would there be a God who can equal the Holy Lord Sri Venkateswara.”
This shloka appears in the Bhavishyattottara Puranam, written by Maharishi Vyasa centuries before the Lord ever came to reside at the Venkatadri Hills.
As per legend, after saving the Earth from Hiranyaksha, Lord Varaha stayed on this hill on the northern bank of Swami Pushkarini. Hence, Tirumala Hills is also referred to as Adivarahakshetra. At the beginning of Kaliyuga, Lord Varaha donated land to Lord Venkateswara at his request. As gratitude, Lord Venkateswara offered the first bell, puja, and Naivedyam to Varahaswamy before they were offered to him. This tradition is still followed today.
